#3069. I reviewed the TCL QM64L — and its bright picture, vibrant colors and great gaming features make it a budget standout

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The TCL QM64L is a solid compact budget Mini-LED TV. It brings great HDR performance, vibrant colors and details, smooth gaming and an improved Fire TV experience. However, you should expect lower black levels, slight blooming and weaker speakers than higher-priced models.

Punchy detail in colors, natural skin tones

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Not everyone has room in their home or dorm room setup for the best 65-inch TVs so finding a smaller, budget-friendly TV that can make movies and shows look great can be challenging. Cheaper TVs can suffer from poor brightness, picture quality, and the smart TV software can be slow and sluggish. The TCL QM64L excels against its rivals in a lot of these categories.

Sporting a sleek, redesigned Fire TV interface and a Mini-LED panel capable of delivering great HDR performance with vibrant colors and natural-looking skin tones, this is a TV that really impresses for its price — $599 for a 65-inch model on Black Friday.

Both in my lab testing and hands-on time, the TCL QM64L consistently delivered an enjoyable viewing experience. However, its compact size and budget-friendly price come with some compromises, including poor black levels, slight blooming around bright highlights and bad downward-firing speakers.

The TCL QM64L might not be taking down mid-tier and high-end flagship TVs when you compare its raw specs and our lab test results, but for budget-conscious buyers who want a small compact TV without breaking the bank, it will deliver a great everyday viewing experience.

The TCL QM64L comes in multiple sizes, starting at 50 inches. You can’t buy the 50-inch size directly from TCL, but third-party retailers like Amazon carry the 50-inch size that we reviewed.

Pricing starts at $499 for the 50-inch model, and goes as high as $2,199 for a 98-inch model. When on sale, you can grab the 50-inch model for $429, and the 98-inch model for $1,699. Full pricing for the range can be seen below.

QD-Mini-LED QLED with Full-Array Local Dimming

Dolby Vision (including Dolby Vision IQ), HDR10+, HDR10, and HLG

144Hz native refresh rate (HDMI 1, 2), 60Hz (HDMI 3,4)

4x HDMI 2.1, 1x USB-A 3.0, 1x USB-A 2.0, ATSC,SPDIF Digital Audio Optical port.

Like many budget TVs, there’s nothing fancy about the design of the TCL QM64L. The only highlight would be its super thin bezels which come in at around a quarter of an inch thick. It also is made of plastic, with legs that attach at a curved angle to support the bottom of the TV. Up front, there’s a silver lip on the bottom of the panel for the TCL logo.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I would have loved for this set to feature center-facing legs like some of its competitors, since that would help save even more space in a tight-packed room. This is not a huge dealbreaker, though, since this TV is already so compact.

What I love the most is that TCL packs in four HDMI 2.1 ports. Two of them — HDMI 1 and HDMI 2 — can output 4K at 144Hz, but the other two are capped at 60Hz. Having two 144Hz ports is nice, especially if you’re a gamer, since you can connect two consoles to the TV. The other ports on the TV include one USB 3.0 port and one USB 2.0 port, as well as the ATSC port, and a SPDIF Digital Audio Optical port.

Whether I was watching “Spider-Man: No Way Home” on our lab’s Blu-Ray player, streaming “Cross” on Amazon Prime Video, or watching a simple SDR aquarium video on YouTube, the Mini-LED panel on this TV produced punchy highlights and plenty of visual pop. However, the weaker black levels and some slight blooming in very specific scenes prevent it from delivering what you might get from a more premium and larger TV.

With “Spider-Man: No Way Home” in Filmmaker Mode, the TCL QM64L was great with fine details, natural skin tones and vibrant colors. Tom Holland’s shirt sported a clean, vibrant blue, while fine details like his facial scar and Zendaya’s red lipstick remained sharp. The TV struggled a bit with overall black levels in the details in the Sanctum Sanctorum undercroft, though. The blacks in Norman Osborne’s jacket and the brickwork felt slightly muted and gray.

In later fight scenes, slight blooming also flared around Spider-Man’s hands as they glowed against dark backgrounds. Punchy silver accents and a shiny gold spider emblem in his Black and Gold Suit, however, proved that the QM64L delivers plenty of visual pop.

When streaming HDR content on Amazon Prime Video, the TCL QM64L wowed me right from the opening seconds in the first episode of “Cross.” Facial textures were impressively rendered, revealing crisp individual strands of beard hair on Cross’s face with that I almost feel the urge to reach out and straighten them.

To my surprise, the QM64L also handled rapid brightness shifts with ease. It seamlessly transitioned from the shadowy, low-light interior of an interrogation room to a dim, moody tunnel intro and then burst into a punchy, bright outdoor shot of the Washington, D.C. skyline.

Finally, switching over to a SDR aquarium video on YouTube, the TCL QM64L continued to impress with its vibrant color handling. As a clownfish navigated through lush pink coral reefs the distinctive white stripe on the clownfish's head popped with crisp, clean brightness against its orange body. This proves that this budget display handles underwater marine scenes with surprising depth and visual punch.

Across all tests, the 50-inch TCL QM64L delivers surprisingly impressive picture quality for a budget TV. It brings out crisp fine details, natural-looking skin tones and vibrant colors across SDR and HDR content.

Roku 65-inch Class Select Series 4K QLED (2026)

Vizio Mini-LED Quantum 4K Smart TV 65-inch VQM65-C

Roku Pro OLED TV 65-inch (Measurements with "Brighter"

I lab-tested the TCL QM64L in filmmaker mode alongside five notable rivals in its class, including the LED-driven Sony Bravia 3 II (65-inch), the the Hisense 65M7SR, the Roku 65-inch Class Select Series 4K QLED (2026), the Vizio Mini-LED Quantum 4K Smart TV 65-inch, and the premium Roku Pro OLED TV 65-inch.

There’s no doubt that this TV will trail its mid-tier and higher-end competitors in raw benchmarking. It is not going to hit high levels of brightness and color accuracy or performance like a flagship might. However, at this price, it is still a surprisingly bright budget TV.

When it comes to the 10% SDR window measurement, which shows you how bright a TV gets with cable TV and everyday content, the Hisense 65M7SR is the best of the bunch at 466 nits. The TCL QM64L follows at 359 nits, and Sony Bravia 3 II hits 352 nits while the Roku Select Series (334 nits) also comes close to that group. The flagship Roku Pro OLED comes in at 330 nits, while the Vizio Mini-LED Quantum trails the group at 218 nits.

My lab assistant and I personally test every TV across SDR and HDR benchmarks using the 10% window method. For color accuracy, we set the TV to Filmmaker Mode, usually the “best” mode on the TV first. We also disable any ambient light sensors that could skew our meter’s readings.

For our tools, we use the Jeti spectraval 1501-HiRes spectroradiometer to profile the Klein K10-A colorimeter. Once profiled, these work with the Murideo 8K-SIX-G Metal pattern generator and a Tom’s-Guide specific workflow in Portrait Displays’ Calman Ultimate software which helps us determine the TV’s overall brightness and color accuracy across HDR and SDR.

We use a Leo Bodnar 4K Video Signal Lag Tester with the TV’s Game Mode to measure how responsive the TV really is. Once all lab testing is done, we put the TV through subjective testing using a curated selection of films and shows, both on streaming services and on our lab’s Blu-ray player.

Visit our “How we test TVs” guide for a more in-depth explanation on the process.

For HDR content, the TCL QM64L shines best with 630 nits in our 10% window test. That puts it ahead of every TV in this comparison group except the Vizio Mini-LED Quantum, which leads at 781 nits.

Color accuracy out of the box in Filmmaker mode is where the TCL QM64L is a little weak. Our lab measured a Delta-E score of 3.3, where lower numbers are better.

With SDR color performance, the TCL fell behind everything except the Roku Select Series, although its results are still respectable considering the prices.

When looking at the UHDA-P3 HDR color gamut coverage, which is how most HDR content is presented, the TCL again fell toward the bottom of the back, only just edging out the Roku Select Series once again.

When it came to the more demanding Rec. 2020 spectrum, the TCL moved up slightly, trailing only the Sony Bravia 3 II and Roku Select Series.

The TCL scored a low result in our input latency tests (13 milliseconds) that put it at the bottom of our test results list, but don't let that fool you: I still enjoyed the gaming experience.

Overall, when battling through a boss fight in Marvel’s Wolverine, I did not experience any lag in my inputs. I also tried playing Sonic Superstars. In this fast-paced game, rolling around collecting coins was fun and super smooth..

Like more premium TVs, TCL bundles in support for VRR, ALLM and Game Accelerator with a Game Bar. All of this meant that when I pressed the menu button on the remote, I could pull up a Game Bar to fine-tune the TV for my gameplay.

Features like Game Picture Mode, Shadow Enhancement, and Aiming Aid can spice up the gaming experience. My personal favorite was the Floating Window option, and High Frame Rate mode, which helped me keep track of the frames when playing Marvel’s Wolverine on our lab’s PlayStation 5.

As mentioned earlier, the TCL QM64L has two HDMI 2.1 ports that support refresh rates of 144Hz; in comparison, the Sony Bravia 3 II and the Roku Pro Series both have four HDMI 2.1 ports, but refresh rates are capped at 120Hz.

Budget TVs have to make some sacrifices, and one of those is the sound setup. The TCL QM64L sports two 10W speakers on the underside front. With the TV sitting on a table, I didn’t quite enjoy the way it handled audio.

While watching “Spider-Man: No Way Home” on our lab’s Blu-ray player, the dialog presentation felt a little muted and muffled from afar. I was forced to push the volume up into the 20s just to make out dialogue clearly.

Listening to "Flower in a Hurricane," from the “Grand Theft Auto 6” trailer, the opening guitars and electronic beats did have some impressive detail and spatial depth. However, as soon as the drum beats kicked in, the bass sounded tinny, hollow, and largely absent.

Pick up one of the best soundbars to upgrade this TV's audio.

One of my biggest complaints about the previous Fire TV interface found on many budget TVs was how outdated it looked, with a giant ad taking up the top of the screen and the navigation bar awkwardly positioned in the middle. Thankfully, Amazon has given its interface a much-needed makeover. The newly redesigned Fire TV OS that came on the QM64L as an out of the box update is super clean, speedy, and brings it up to par with what I’ve seen on other SmartTV platforms this year.

The navigation bar now sits at the top of the screen, with clearly labeled sections for profile, search, home, movies, TV Shows, live, sports and news. It's a much more intuitive layout that I’ve long enjoyed on Google TV and even Samsung’s Tizen OS.

Of course, the ads are still there. Show recommendations and promotional content now take up the space where the old navigation bar used to sit. There's also a dedicated Apps and Channels section, making it easier to jump straight into your favorite streaming services.

The redesigned interface feels more fluid. I frequently dive into the picture settings when testing TVs, and I appreciate how the new menus use a gray background with white highlights to make it easier to see which setting you're adjusting. It's a small change, but one that makes the interface feel considerably more polished.

This TV also has a cool ambient mode that displays artwork when you're not actively watching something. It's a nice touch that gives the QM64L a little more personality when it's not in use. I love it, and I am sure students putting this TV in a dorm room will too.

The remote included with this TV is nothing fancy. While it is backlit, it has the same standard layout as many remotes that come with TCL’s other TVs. I like the dedicated play and pause button, as well as the buttons for accessing the settings, and Netflix and YouTube. A programmable button would have been nice, but you can’t expect that for this price.

The TCL QM64L is a great 50-inch TV. For budget-conscious buyers, the QM64L delivers where it counts most. Its Mini-LED brightness, attention to fine details, and sleek Fire TV OS helps it stand out as one of the best compact TV values for small living rooms, bedrooms, or dorm setups.

The biggest rival would be the Hisense 65M7SR with its better SDR brightness, slightly more accurate out-of-box color performance, and slightly wider color gamut coverage than the TCL QM64L. While it can't match the TCL's HDR brightness, it's just as compelling an option if you prefer the Roku TV experience and want to prioritize overall color performance over bright HDR.

The QM64L’s budget price tag does come with clear trade-offs like muted, grayish blacks, and slight blooming around bright objects in dark scenes. The downward-firing speakers also deliver hollow audio with muddy dialogue, making a soundbar an essential purchase.

While it is more expensive, the Sony Bravia 3 II still serves as a major step up from this TCL thanks to Sony's superior image processing and color accuracy. Finally, if your main goal is better HDR brightness in a sunlit room, the Vizio Mini-LED Quantum will be for you.

Of course, if budget isn't a strict constraint and you want to completely eliminate blooming with infinite contrast and pristine color, stepping up to an OLED like the Roku Pro Series OLED is the ultimate fix for many of these TVs problems, though it comes at a higher cost.

But, if you're looking for an affordable set under $500, the TCL QM64L could be just the ticket.

#3068. London startup Sequent raises $2.2M to mathematically prove code safe

Backers include Metaplanet, the firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic's 2021 Series A.

Sequent co-founders Ramana Kumar (left) and Charles Cooper at the Alan Turing memorial, after whom the company’s product Alan is named.

Sequent, a London startup that uses mathematical proof to show software obeys its safety rules, has raised $2.2M in pre-seed funding. Frachtis co-led the round with Metaplanet, the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, the man who led Anthropic’s 2021 Series A.

Its product, Alan, goes after what testing cannot do. A test checks the cases someone thought to try, while a formal proof shows the code follows its rules in every case. Writing proofs by hand takes specialists months or years, which has kept the method locked up in fields like aircraft controls.

AI has changed that maths, as the models suit the repetitive grind that proofs demand. With Alan, engineers state their safety rules in plain language, such as no user being able to withdraw more than their balance.

The AI then hunts for the proofs, and a separate checker called HOL4, which uses no AI, confirms every step or throws the proof out.

The company was born from a costly mistake: the CEO, Charles Cooper, who leads Vyper, one of the two main programming languages on Ethereum, in 2021 he accidentally introduced a flaw into its compiler. In July 2023, attackers used that bug to drain more than $60mn from older pools at the exchange Curve and other projects.

After the attack, Ramana Kumar, a former Google DeepMind safety researcher, offered to help prove the compiler correct. He had formed, having co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct down to the instructions a computer runs, and the work grew into Sequent, where he is now CTO.

Curve has become the first paying customer. For one type of its pools, Alan has proved that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order.

Whenever the pool’s code changes, “we can prove depositors’ money stays protected by the same limit,” Curve CEO Michael Egorov said in a statement.

Cooper argues the lesson reaches well beyond crypto. Banks and governments have long leaned on keeping their old code private, he says. AI-powered attacks are eroding that shield, while cheap proofs hand the advantage back to defenders.

Crucially, AI never gets the final word. At DeepMind, Kumar studied how AI finds shortcuts that satisfy a rule’s letter while missing its point. So engineers sign off on every rule themselves, and each proof must pass HOL4, whose core is small enough for experts to inspect line by line.

Alan works on Vyper smart contracts today, with Solidity and Solana support in development and Rust, C, TypeScript, and Python on the roadmap. Early access starts at $99 a month, and the founders’ next target is the Vyper compiler itself, the place where the original flaw lived.

#3067. Apple Mail added four convenient new features in iOS 27

iOS 27 brought new features to Apple Wallet, Maps, Notes, Messages, and more—and it includes key upgrades for the Mail app too. Here’s everything new for Apple Mail in iOS 27.

If you have much history using Apple Mail, you’ll know that its search feature hasn’t always been the best. But in iOS 27, search has gotten a big upgrade.

More relevant search in Mail. A new ranking system brings the most relevant results to the top to help you find what you need right away — even if it’s buried deep in your inbox.

I can’t count the number of times search has previously failed to find messages that I knew existed. So far in my usage, iOS 27 has fixed that.

Suggestions at the top of messages have been in Apple Mail for years. But in iOS 27, they have a new, more flexible design and expand to support third-party apps.

When Mail detects that you might want to take action on the contents of an email, a suggestion might appear at the top of the message. These include: directions in Maps, creating events in Calendar, tracking a shipment with Apple Wallet, and more.

In iOS 27, third-party apps can offer suggestions too. And when multiple apps are available with suggested actions, there’s a drop-down menu to show you all available options.

Smart Reply is a keyboard feature that automatically surfaces reply options you can utilize with a single tap.

In iOS 27, the next generation of Apple Intelligence comes with improvements to Smart Reply.

Apple says that Smart Reply “can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.” Essentially, rather than offering fairly generic reply options, now Smart Reply suggestions will actually sound a lot more like you.

Apple has added ‘Ask Siri’ buttons throughout Apple Mail, just like the rest of its system apps. And Siri AI brings a bunch of new powers for Mail users.

One example I’ve seen several times on social media is that you can ask Siri to delete all messages from a specific sender that’s spamming you.

I asked the new Siri on iOS 27 to delete Spam emails from a particular adddess and it just did that so seamlessly pic.twitter.com/EYn74buYAX

#3066. Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab CEO on How He Reached the C-Suite

Anthony Vetro’s journey from multimedia pioneer to executive

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

At the 2025 IEEE Vision, Innovation, and Challenges Summit, IEEE Fellow Anthony Vetro discusses the need for open innovation models to keep pace with rapid technological change taking place at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories.

The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since.

Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

Anthony Vetro Employer Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.Title President and CEO Member grade FellowAlma mater Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.

Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation.

Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration.

His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO.

He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe.

Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says.

“Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says.

Vetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island.

Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age.

“My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications.

“Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.”

Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School, a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field.

“A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says.

He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994.

“As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.”

It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes.

“I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.”

“The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.”

After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

“The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says.

He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems.

Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working.

“That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001.

After six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018.

“After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.”

He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them.

To help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston, its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL.

The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan.

The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering, according to the company’s website. Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.”

The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up.

Vetro says he’s excited about the endeavor.

“Serendie Street [Boston] aims to strengthen the bridge between our global R&D efforts and real-world industry challenges. The hub is intended to bring our partners and customers together to engage in more cocreation activities, where we listen to their problems and work together to solve them,” he says. “I think the company has come to recognize that we can’t just do it all internally by ourselves.”

The technologies being worked on include robotics, energy solutions such as integrating renewable energy into the grid, and more energy-efficient data center systems.

The decision to colocate the hub with MERL offices was deliberate, Vetro says.

“The area has a very rich ecosystem,” he says. “We have Harvard, MIT, and many other universities a stone’s throw away.”

Vetro joined IEEE in 1992 as a student member during an event the Polytechnic’s student branch was holding. He enjoyed reading the IEEE Potentials student member publication and other periodicals, he says.

“In the earliest stages of my career, IEEE was a place where I could attend conferences, read journals, and stay on top of the latest research and trends,” he says. “Over the years, I was able to build a professional network, which has been helpful. That facilitated a lot of research collaboration with university professors attending the conferences.

“In more recent years, IEEE has provided a great platform for industry to exhibit thought leadership and discuss real-world problems we’re facing. I think these discussions may have even set some research directions among the academic community.”

Vetro is an active volunteer for the IEEE Signal Processing Society. He has chaired several of its technical committees and conferences, and he served as an associate editor for some of its journals.

He says he’s most proud of establishing the society’s industry board and serving as its inaugural chair. The board formed a corporate engagement program, launched the Industry Signals newsletter, developed short courses tailored to industry, and holds career fairs at the society’s flagship conferences.

Vetro also had a hand in MERL sponsoring two IEEE technical field awards: the Flanagan Speech and Audio Processing Award and the Fourier Award for Signal Processing.

“Industry-level engagement in IEEE is really very vital to the organization in maintaining its relevance to the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity,” he says.

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

#3062. Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft announced two new AI models at Ignite 2026 that promise impressive performance for much lower cost. They could reshape its relationship with OpenAI and Anthropic for good.

At today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the company introduced two new frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model shows 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Microsoft says MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

This doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

It’s also important to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

Throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft showed slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these new models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex

One thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the company paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the company’s vast product line.

If you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As users adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous

There’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

This becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

Think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the company itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a company is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these new models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first

A company with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

There’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Microsoft says the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

Benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the new models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open issue.

The company also described clearly that these new models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. You’re probably not going to use them to solve a decades-old mathematics challenge. But you’re very likely to use them to reformat your PowerPoint.

Speaking of reformatting your PowerPoint, Microsoft also emphasized that these new models did unusually well on visualization assignments. That’s a very good fit for not only UI design challenges but also graphics and slide production.

#3061. Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft could reshape enterprise spending, but there's a critical difference between estimated value and money saved.

We all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

If it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s big bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

Instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

Then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s new

What comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

There’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically says, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”

In other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving company labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the company saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your company needs a chief AI officer in 2026

I find it particularly telling that this is from the company that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

That’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

Microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the company’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the company’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:

This means the company doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

#3060. Berkshire Hit a Record High While AI Power Stocks Sold Off. Here’s What That Says About Where Energy Money Is Going.

Berkshire Hathaway rose as stocks like Bloom Energy and Caterpillar dropped, suggesting safety is increasingly important.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 24, 2026 at 6:42PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›

Over the past three months, Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.73%)(BRKB +0.85%) is up roughly 15% as of this writing. By comparison, Bloom Energy (BE -6.98%) and Caterpillar (CAT -1.17%), both headline-grabbing artificial intelligence (AI) energy plays, are down 29% and 38%, respectively. Investors aren't giving up on the companies that provide energy for AI, but they may be shifting toward more conservative investments. Here's what you need to know.

Artificial intelligence is really just a fancy computer program. Without electricity, it can't exist. But AI uses a tremendous amount of power, resulting in consumer backlash against the data centers that host it. This is why investors have been so attracted to Bloom Energy and Caterpillar.

Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells. These factory-produced items can be placed wherever they are needed to provide off-grid power. Caterpillar, while best known for its heavy earth-moving equipment, also makes generators that provide off-grid power. However, given the backlash against AI, investor enthusiasm for AI stocks has diminished, and these stocks have fallen alongside the broader AI trade despite still-high expectations for power demand.

Meanwhile, Berkshire Hathaway's shares have been on the rise. That is at least partly a flight-to-safety trade. Berkshire Hathaway is a giant conglomerate with businesses ranging from insurance to homebuilding, and much in between. It also has more than $370 billion in cash sitting on its balance sheet to cushion it against a market downturn. That cash also provides it with the ability to buy if a bear market opens up attractive investment opportunities.

That's a good start, but there's another small wrinkle here. Over the last three months, Southern Company (SO +1.07%), a large regulated U.S. utility, is up nearly 5%, and Kinder Morgan (KMI +1.67%), a large North American pipeline operator, is down just 2%. These businesses will both be integral to powering AI. They aren't as exciting as Bloom Energy or Cat, but that's the point right now. Investors are looking for a safe haven as AI enthusiasm hits a road bump and are shifting toward boring, reliable businesses.

Notably, Southern offers a reliable 3.2% dividend yield, while Kinder Morgan's yield is 3.9%. Berkshire Hathaway doesn't pay a dividend; however, two of its largest divisions are its utility and energy segments. Add that to the rest of the company's owned business portfolio and its large collection of publicly traded stocks, and you have diversification along with continued exposure to the growing demand for electricity. This is not a small matter, given that electricity demand increased by 10% between 2005 and 2025 and is projected to grow by 60% between 2025 and 2045.

Basically, Berkshire Hathaway could offer the best of both worlds. You own a diversified and financially strong company that is prepared to take advantage of a bear market. And you continue to have exposure to AI's growing appetite for power. All in one investment. Investors may not be dumping AI power companies; they may just be getting more selective and conservative.

The caveat here is that Berkshire Hathaway is now trading near all-time highs. However, the company has been buying back its own stock over the last two quarters, which it has historically done only when it believes the stock is trading below its intrinsic value. While it probably isn't fair to suggest Berkshire Hathaway is a deep-value opportunity, if you are looking for a safer way to play long-term energy demand from AI, the company itself thinks its stock is attractive. It's probably worth a deep dive, even if you only end up putting it on your wish list.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The company also released new ROI tracking tools for companies monitoring their AI spend.

AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring.

During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several new Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets, which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework.

“As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft said. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.”

Microsoft also announced Autopilot, a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described.

In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots, but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft said, and assign it tasks.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s new Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector

Microsoft said the agent will be able to autonomously handle “meetings and follow-ups on its own,” though that claim may be best verified by teams themselves.

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

“Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft said.

The company added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

Nadella also announced a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. Currently in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up quickly,” Microsoft said of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Microsoft also announced that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can quickly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft announced a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Agent 365, which Microsoft announced last year, is the company’s observability platform. Microsoft said Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft showed how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

“It starts with a new way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft said. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

“Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft said. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise plans.

Last week, OpenAI introduced GPT-6.2, its latest generation of AI models, with some impressive capabilities for coding, research and tackling complex projects. But for those of us who use ChatGPT for everything from planning dinner to troubleshooting tech problems, this week's update might be even more useful.

OpenAI is bringing a version of GPT-6.2 Sol to the regular Chat tab, so you no longer need to switch to ChatGPT Work to benefit from some of the company's latest AI improvements.

According to OpenAI's release notes, ChatGPT is now better at making sense of images, handling complicated requests and searching the web. It can also recognize when you might benefit from a little extra help, such as keeping an eye on the price of a product you've been meaning to buy.

One of the biggest improvements is how well ChatGPT understands images. In OpenAI's internal testing, GPT-6.2 scored 71.7%, up from 47.4% with GPT-6. It also handled particularly challenging instructions with a 78.1% success rate, compared with 62.5% for the previous model.

Benchmarks are one thing, but I'm more interested in what these improvements mean when you're using ChatGPT in your everyday life.

One of the most frustrating things about using AI to organize your life is when it overlooks an important detail. You might give ChatGPT a dozen things you need to accomplish, only to discover that its carefully organized schedule doesn't account for travel time or the fact that you need to be in two places at once.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

GPT-6.2's improved instruction following could make it more reliable when juggling competing priorities. The key is to give ChatGPT multiple constraints that require it to think through the problem rather than simply organize a list.

Try this prompt: Help me organize Thanksgiving morning. Dinner is at 3 p.m., my turkey needs four hours in the oven and 30 minutes to rest, my sides need different oven temperatures and I need an hour to get ready. Create a realistic schedule, flag any conflicts and build in extra time in case something goes wrong.

ChatGPT has been able to analyze photos for years, but its ability to interpret smaller details and understand how objects relate to one another hasn't always been consistent.

With the latest upgrade, it's worth revisiting some of the visual tasks that may have disappointed you in the past. Take a picture of a cluttered kitchen cabinet, your refrigerator or even the tangled cables behind your TV.

Try this prompt: Analyze this photo and identify three changes I could make to improve this space without buying anything new. Base your suggestions only on what you can actually see, and tell me if you're uncertain about anything.

With Black Friday deals already happening now, the timing of ChatGPT's improved web research capabilities couldn't be better.

Instead of asking the chatbot to find the cheapest version of a product, give it a more complicated shopping decision that requires it to weigh several factors.A useful response should go beyond rounding up products. It should explain why certain features matter for your particular home and whether spending more would actually make a difference.

Remember to verify prices and availability before making a purchase.

Try this prompt: Find the three best robot vacuum deals currently available for under $300. I have pets, hardwood floors and several area rugs. Prioritize obstacle avoidance and pet hair pickup over flashy features. Check current prices, compare independent reviews and explain which one offers the best value. Include links to your sources.

You don't always need AI to write something from scratch. Sometimes, the more valuable skill is its ability to understand exactly what you want changed without touching everything else.

The improvements to GPT-6.2's instruction following could be useful for anyone who has asked ChatGPT to make a minor edit, only to receive a completely rewritten document.

Paste in an email, holiday letter or piece of writing you've been working on. This is a surprisingly demanding task for an AI model because it requires restraint as much as writing ability.

Try this prompt: Edit this for clarity without changing my personality or writing style. Keep my opening and closing sentences exactly as they are. Don't add new information, don't make it more formal and don't rewrite sentences that already work. Show me the revised version and briefly explain your three most significant changes.

One of the more interesting improvements in this update has less to do with the quality of ChatGPT's immediate answers and more to do with what happens after the conversation.

OpenAI says the chatbot is better at identifying situations where ongoing assistance might be useful. For example, instead of repeatedly checking whether a product has gone on sale, you could ask ChatGPT to monitor it. Depending on your account's available features, ChatGPT may offer to set up an automated price check. Make sure you confirm that the task has actually been created rather than assuming the chatbot will continue monitoring something on its own.

Try this prompt: I'm interested in buying a Kindle Scribe, but I don't want to pay full price. Find the best available deal today and offer to notify me if the price drops below $250 before Christmas.

With the newest update, OpenAI is focusing on some of the everyday frustrations that can make AI feel like more work than it's worth.

Having to repeat instructions, correct misunderstood images or double-check research can quickly undermine the time-saving benefits of using an AI assistant.

If GPT-6.2 can reduce those frustrations, this upgrade could be a productivity improvement for the average ChatGPT user.

#3056. Microsoft’s new Licensed Weights lets businesses customize AI models with their own data

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft is bridging the gap between proprietary and open-weight AI while targeting data-conscious businesses.

During the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company. But new model releases are almost a dime a dozen these days, and accelerating fast — what really stood out was how Microsoft will let its customers access those models.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5

MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

“You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, said during the keynote.

The approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft said it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman said during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

The dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the company has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman said of the new coding model the company announced at Ignite.

The company also released its new image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

The Superscore is an AI-powered score that evaluates a company's overall strength by combining financial performance, product market position, technological capabilities, leadership quality, and relative valuation. It represents the unification of all our scores into a single score for public companies, with five rating bands: Exceptional (90-100), Strong (75-89), Above Average (60-74), Average (40-59), and Cautious (0-39). Domino's next phase of growth will likely rhyme with its first. Geographic expansion, this time internationally, will be critical. Ah, the Bulgarian split squat. Feared by many, loathed by most, but loved by personal trainers all over the world. What if I told you that you'd enjoy this lower-body exercise infinitely more if you followed three simple steps to fix up your form?

It's surprisingly easy to make mistakes with this leg-day exercise, and really, it can be adjusted to be more quad-dominant or glute-dominant — but there are clear signs of bad form, and many more people than you'd think end up on the physical therapy couch because of poor lifting mechanics.

To maximize the benefits of this weightlifting exercise, I recommend learning how to do the Bulgarian split squat before bad habits set in. As a trainer, I have a few tips to help you. Scroll on to see if you're making these common mistakes below and my top tips to fix your form fast.

A post shared by Tom's Guide Fitness | Workout Tips & Gear (@tomsguidefitness)

It's a compound exercise and a part of functional training workouts and strength programs everywhere, helping you build strength and muscle in your glutes, hips, quads, hamstrings and core.

The move requires balance and coordination, while your upper body, core and hips help stabilize you as you move. But people tend to think of this move as more quads than glutes, which isn't exactly the case.

Here's what I see go wrong, and three quick fixes:

In short, you're wasting your time if your form is badly off. And we're busy humans who don't like our time being wasted, right?

Leaning back too far removes tension from the working muscles and overloads your lower back. Keep your torso static and stable — don't hunch or allow your knees to cave inward. That means engaging your core and using the power of your core, glutes and legs to drive movement.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Next, think about your gravity; as I mentioned, keep your back straight and slightly hinge forward to help engage the glutes on your standing leg. If you work with a weight in your opposite hand, this will engage more of the outer glutes, or gluteus medius.

Taking time during the eccentric contraction means slowing down the lowering phase; you can then press upward with power while maximizing tension. It's now thought, due to advances in research, that eccentric contraction is important for muscle growth and braking force.

If you have an injury, pre-existing health conditions, or you experience pain, speak with a qualified personal trainer or physician first.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

I've been using Ubuntu 27.04, and the speed boost is noticeable. Here's what else is coming.

Ubuntu 27.04, Tenacious T-Rex, is set for an April 22, 2027 release. Although that seems a long way off, it’s sooner than you think. As is implied by the release number, 27.04 is not an LTS release, so it only receives support for nine months (until January 2028). The good news is that you can migrate from 27.04 to 27.10, and then to the LTS release, 28.04. The entire upgrade path ensures that you don’t have to miss a single release.

But what’s coming in Ubuntu 27.04? Given that it’s an interim release, you’re probably assuming that there’ll be nothing exciting to be found. Although there won’t be any game-changing additions, there will be plenty of refinements and bug fixes.

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet

I’ve been using the daily release of Ubuntu 27.04 for a bit. Let’s take a look at what is currently expected in Tenacious T-Rex.

This is probably the biggest addition to the next release of Ubuntu. And although you won’t find any major changes in GNOME, there are some important ones. First off, there will be editable quick settings, which allow for customizing, adding, removing, and rearranging toggles and widgets. GNOME 52 will also enjoy a revamped calendar popover, which streamlines the feature to focus primarily on events, time, and weather.

Also: Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why

There will also be several improvements to window management, such as a spatial overview and a mosaic/tiling system for auto-resizing and organizing windows, a refined full-screen Alt+Tab app switcher, which will be capable of grouping older windows by application while showing newer ones individually, and finally, the ability to remember window sizing, placement, and workspace.

Desktop search is also getting a bit of polish by way of a redesigned popover and an improved results overlay that includes file previews, multiple actions, and search filters. And, as usual, there will be plenty of bug fixes and performance enhancements. The bump in speed is noticeable, too, in my testing.

Ubuntu 27.04 will ship with the Linux 7.6 kernel, which includes better VRAM management for gaming and expanded support for modern hardware, such as early enablement for AMD Zen 6, stable support for Intel Xe3P, mainline boot capabilities for Apple M3 Pro/Max/Ultra, and initial support for the 2026 Steam Controller.

There will also be performance gains for both the Btrfs and Ext4 file systems, which (along with the improvements in GNOME 52) will make Ubuntu 27.04 one of the best-performing releases in some time.

Also: This lightweight Linux distro revives old PCs destined for the junk pile – and it’s beautiful

One thing that surprised me is that Myna (Ubuntu’s AI dictation tool) has yet to find its way into the Ubuntu ISO as a default app. As with Ubuntu 26.10, you can install it, but you have to first add the necessary repository with:

With the repository added, you can install it with:

Once installed, you can use it as expected.

As of right now, that’s all we know about Tenacious T-Rex.

It’s so early in the release cycle that it still uses the default 26.10 wallpaper, but there will be more information soon. I will say this: I’ve come to count on Ubuntu’s latest releases to be an improvement over the previous iterations, and from what I’ve seen so far in my testing, 27.04 will not disappoint. It may not knock you back to prehistoric times, but Tenacious T-Rex will wow you with its performance and polished looks.

Also: Linux has hundreds of distros: 5 reasons to stop using the same few

It’s been a very long time since Canonical had a disappointing release, and 27.04 will keep up that trend.
