#3043. Netflix Stock Is Down 37% in 2026, But the Business Is Still Growing. Here's Why I'd Buy It Before the End of November.

Netflix stock is down 56% from its summer 2025 peak. Here's what the sell-off may be missing about the thriving business.

By Anders Bylund – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:07PM EST

Media-streaming veteran Netflix (NFLX +1.32%) is on the outs with Wall Street again. The stock reached all-time highs in the summer of 2025, as investors forgave the company for the canceled, expensive Warner Bros. buyout idea. As of Nov. 24, Netflix stock is down 56% from that peak, including a 37% year-to-date drop.

And the more I look at the drooping stock chart, the more I scratch my head in confusion. The business keeps growing, video streaming remains a healthy global market, and Netflix's stock isn't even expensive.

Third-quarter results did not look like those of a company in trouble. Revenue rose 11.8% to $12.9 billion. Operating income jumped 37.3% to $4.5 billion, and operating margin widened to 34.6% from 28.2% in the year-ago period. Management guided for 2026 revenue of $51.1 billion, up 13%, and an operating margin of 31.5%, versus 29.5% in 2025. That's a combo of double-digit revenue growth and widening margins.

Investors sold anyway. The stock fell as much as 6.7% the next morning, and several analysts trimmed their price targets. At first glance, the reasons look fair. Netflix cut its 2026 advertising revenue forecast from roughly $3 billion to about $2.7 billion, citing slower rollout of some new ad products. Ad revenue is still on pace to grow more than 80% this year, per co-CEO Greg Peters. Management conceded, though, that view-hour growth needs to improve and that the U.S. content group can do better.

"Our [U.S.] engagement is solid, and it will allow us to continue to grow as we have for the last several years, but we know that we can do better. And that better is our upside," Peters said on the earnings call. "It's our goal to go from very good to great on the performance of that slate."

Now check the stock's price tag. Netflix's market cap is about $238.6 billion. Tack on $7.1 billion of net debt, and the whole enterprise costs about 15.8 times the operating income it generated over the past four quarters. That's a low multiple for a company that turned 31.3% of its revenue into operating income over the past year. Take a quick look at the price chart and you'd assume the business was shrinking. Well, it's not.

Management has been voting with the checkbook, so to speak. Netflix bought back 63.9 million shares for $4.8 billion last quarter (a company record, narrowly edging the Q2 buyback budget) at an average of about $75 per stub. The stock now sits around $59, so the timing could have been better. Still, $22.3 billion of buyback authorization remains, against $8.2 billion of cash and about $12.0 billion of expected 2026 free cash flow. Netflix has leaned harder into buybacks as the stock has slid this year, and the remaining authorization leaves room for more:

NFLX data by YCharts. The chart shows quarterly buybacks; Netflix reported $4.8 billion for Q3 2026.

Wall Street has not given up on the story. The analyst consensus rating is Buy, and short-sellers hold roughly 2% of Netflix's shares, a thin bearish bet against the stock.

The fourth quarter should keep the content engine busy. Netflix calls it the biggest quarterly live slate it has ever scheduled, including its first NFL Thanksgiving Eve game on Nov. 25. That game kicks off a stretch of live events that could shift sentiment fast: a Christmas Day football doubleheader and the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua heavyweight boxing event. Self-produced entertainment releases include "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," a new season of "The Diplomat," and the sixth and final run of "Emily in Paris."

Netflix also plans to launch its advertising tier in 15 more countries next year, starting in March. It recently named former Disney (DIS +1.86%) executive Peter Rice as chief content officer. Regional hits matter, too; Netflix has a deep bench of local producers, and their shows are moving the needle. For instance, India view hours grew 24% in the third quarter while revenue there rose about 18% on a currency-neutral basis.

I can't pretend that Netflix is a risk-free investment. Some new ad products are behind schedule. Fourth-quarter margin guidance of 26% absorbs about 120 basis points of cost from headcount cuts. Operating income is guided to about $3.5 billion, up 18.4% from a year ago, and that's a sharp slowdown from the third quarter's 37.3% jump. The U.S. slate needs to start landing home runs instead of base hits, which is exactly the job Peter Rice just inherited. So no, you shouldn't bet the farm, the cat, and the horse it rode in on. A normal slice of a diversified portfolio is plenty.

But a growing, cash-generating business at about 16 times operating income, with a Buy consensus and almost nobody shorting it? That's why I'd buy Netflix now, rather than wait for the holiday slate to change the market mood. The stock may keep sliding in the short term; the business, so far, is not.

#3041. I Put Xiaomi’s 18 Pro Max Camera to the Test and I Love the Results

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Xiaomi's bonkers dual-screen phone is here and I've tested its camera.

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Xiaomi has taken the wraps off its latest 18 Pro Max Android phone in Paris. I’ve had the phone for the past few weeks and have been putting the camera to the test in my beautiful home of Edinburgh, Scotland, as well as on the beautiful (and rainy) streets of Paris. You can check out my review of the phone if you’re keen to hear more about that wild rear screen on the back, but here I wanted to share some of my favorite photos I’ve taken with the phone so far.

The images seen here are taken with the phone’s various built-in camera modes, largely the black and white mode, as I love the dramatic, filmic look it produces. They’re presented either as-shot or with minimal adjustments using the phone’s built-in editing tools.

Taken using one of the phone’s built-in color styles, I love the vibrancy in this shot. The reds really pop, while the wider angle of the main camera emphasizes the tunnel effect of the alleyway, drawing the eye to the person and their dog.

I may be spoiling the rest of the images here by saying that this is my absolute favorite shot I’ve taken, but there we go. I took this using one of the dedicated black-and-white modes, and I think the tones here are perfect. Excellent dynamic range and contrast, and just the right amount of film grain. I positioned the figure between the buildings and had the phone almost on the floor to turn the rain-soaked tiles into a reflective surface to add some drama to this scene. I then applied a wide cinematic crop in post to give it that extra edge. Lovely stuff.

Most of my favorite photos with the phone were taken using the black-and-white mode. It’s no surprise; I shoot in black and white very often on my Leica Q3 43, and I used the monochrome mode for my favorite shots with Xiaomi’s Leitzphone earlier in the year.

The phone captures excellent black-and-white photos at night, too.

And by exposing for the bright highlights in this scene, I was able to create this stark, moody image of my handsome orange cat, Toulouse. Is he the best cat you’ve ever seen? Of course he is.

Back in color, this UFO that had presumably crash-landed in this Parisian market looks great in this filmic color mode. The oranges and reds pop against the other tones in this scene.

While this quick street portrait is similarly punchy.

I used manual mode here, taking full control over the white balance and exposure settings to achieve the tones I wanted. It’s a great-looking shot with excellent dynamic range. Xiaomi’s phone doesn’t appear to go too hard with its software processing either, meaning that even fine details look quite natural. Other Android phone-makers could take note.

As with the photo of Toulouse the cat, I exposed for the highlights here, forcing the rest of the scene under this bridge into shadow. As a result, it looks moody and dramatic but crucially it also looks exactly as I hoped it would. Many phones would try to artificially lift the shadows here, which would ruin the vibe I was going for.

I took this with the phone’s telephoto zoom lens, aiming to focus more on the digger as the subject and use the water for reflection. I love how this shot looks, especially in black and white, as the cloud detail behind it is especially noticeable.

While here I used the full wide angle of the main camera in order to create a lot of negative space around the figures, emphasizing the size of the building around them.

That building was Le Grande Arche in Paris and despite it being a miserably cold, wet and cloudy day I think the phone has captured a satisfyingly stark scene here.

I don’t like flying, so I distracted myself on the flight out to Paris by taking photos of things with the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, including this man having a look out of the window.

And this shot of my plane’s wing somewhere above the UK. Again, in black and white. When it looks this good, why would I choose anything else?

And while we’re still in black and white, a particularly friendly pigeon. Hi, friend!

And to round us off, this dude in shades looking at a menu.

I’m genuinely really thrilled with so many of the shots I’ve taken with this phone. The black-and-white mode in particular is spectacular, and I’m looking forward to taking more shots with it over the coming weeks and months.

Editors’ note: Andrew Lanxon’s travel costs to attend Xiaomi’s launch event in Paris were covered by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

#3040. Most Stocks Are Losers. Here's How You Can Still Win

Seek out and invest in the best. Learn from the rest.

By Joe Tenebruso – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:21PM EST

Many of your stocks are likely to disappoint you.

It's a sobering statement, but one that's borne out by decades of stock market returns.

Research from J.P. Morgan going back to 1980 shows that two-thirds of the stocks in the Russell 3000, which is designed to track the performance of the largest 3,000 publicly traded U.S. companies, tend to underperform the index.

Worse still, roughly 40% of stocks had negative absolute returns.

Moreover, a report from Trivariate Research suggests that an even larger percentage of companies underperformed in recent years, with just 23% of stocks beating the S&P 500 over the past decade.

At first glance, this data is pretty disheartening. Investing may not be easy, but this research makes it seem nearly impossible to be successful.

The truth, fortunately, is that it's not.

There's a beautiful asymmetry to investing.

It's true that a stock could lose 100% of its value. Enduring such a loss is not pleasant. But a well-chosen stock can gain 200%, 500%, or even 1,000% or more.

This capped downside and uncapped upside is part of the magic of investing. As long as you don't use leverage (such as buying stocks on margin), a few big winners can more than make up for a host of losers.

While the odds may be against you, it's still possible to find stocks that go on to outperform the market averages.

The most valuable suggestion I can give you is to buy shares in the best businesses you can find.

Search for companies with the strongest competitive advantages and largest growth opportunities. This includes those with proven business models, beloved brands, superior products and services, and excellent management. Even better if they also possess powerful network effects, high barriers to entry, and sizable switching costs.

Look for the innovators, disruptors, and best of breed. I call these businesses Tier 1 enterprises, and finding just a handful of them can set you up for a lifetime of investment success.

To achieve those life-changing returns, you'll need to keep them long enough to maximize their impact on your wealth. This is one reason why Warren Buffett says his "favorite holding period is forever."

Strive to purchase only shares of businesses you plan to hold for many years. This will lead you to focus on companies with the strongest competitive positions and widest economic moats, or those you believe will eventually build them.

Still, despite your best efforts, you will make mistakes. Don't let them derail you.

A stock you thought was a sure winner will fail. Recessions will slow the greatest of growth stories. Bear markets will bring fear, uncertainty, and doubt. Even your own emotions may betray you.

Come what may, don't quit. Steel yourself with the knowledge that the hard times will pass and you will get through them.

Learn from your mistakes. Apply the lessons to your future stock selections.

Continuously refine your investing process until you obtain the results you need to provide for yourself and your family and achieve your financial freedom.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Home Entertainment > Media Streamers

Fans of the Roku Aquatic Life screensaver will need to find a new way to just keep swimming.

Roku users may be getting that sinking feeling, as the platform is retiring its classic animated Aquatic Life screensaver.

The popular animation featuring realistic aquarium life will be replaced by the Roku City screensaver on Dec. 1. Roku City is the platform’s signature purple skyline, featuring rotating digital billboards packed with brand sponsorships and clever pop-culture Easter eggs. (Seattle’s short-spined raccoon, Jimothy, has made an appearance.)

That doesn’t mean all fish-filled options have been flushed. Several third-party Roku wallpaper apps offer a variety of aquarium options to choose from. But if you’re sticking to what Roku itself provides on its streaming boxes, the move away from the aquarium screensaver also means switching to an alternative that’s filled with advertising.

“It seems like this is a way for Roku to convert a popular screensaver into a way to make money, or at least generate more engagement, via the Roku City version,” said CNET Senior Editor Ty Pendlebury, who covers home entertainment options including the Roku streaming boxes.

A Roku representative didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Viewers who miss these specific fish can still watch a YouTube version of Roku’s Aquatic Life screensaver for as long as the company chooses to keep this nearly 3-minute video on the internet.

The Aquatic Life screensaver loss is a drop in the ocean compared to other changes at the streamer this year. Roku was purchased by Fox for $22 billion in June, which puts the streaming platform under the same ownership as Fox’s Tubi and Fox One channels. That deal is expected to close in 2027.

#3037. Google Wallet comes to your iPhone – but without this feature

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > iOS

The new Google Wallet app brings Gemini agentic shopping to US-based iOS users - sorry, no tap-to-pay.

The Google Wallet app is available for iPhone users in the US for the first time. iOS users who download the new Google Wallet app can manage online payments for faster checkout at places that support Google Pay. However, Apple restricts Google’s ability to offer tap-to-pay service on the iOS app, so users won’t be able to use Google Wallet for contactless checkout on iPhone.

Also: You can use Google’s Spark AI agent, renamed Tasks, for free now – with limits

The new Google Wallet app lets you digitize physical cards, including payment, loyalty, and membership cards, as well as boarding passes. Google Wallet app users on iOS will also be able to view receipts and track orders pulled from Gmail in one app.

There used to be a Google Pay app for iOS, but it was discontinued in 2024. The old Google Pay app also didn’t support tap-to-pay on iPhone, but it offered limited functionality, including support for loyalty and gift cards, as well as purchase tracking.

The biggest difference between the old Google Pay app for iOS and the new Google Wallet is the AI component, which supports agentic shopping, likely as Google’s longer-term play.

One of Google’s goals for the Wallet app on iOS is to make it a central place to manage purchases made by its AI agents. The Agents section in Google Wallet for iPhone lets you manage and monitor purchases made through Gemini.

Agentic commerce is on the rise, as evidenced by the growing use of Meta’s Muse. Gemini can make purchases and payments through the Tasks feature, which lets you give Gemini permission to buy the items you want and set your maximum budget.

Also: Google Wallet just turned your Android phone into a digital house key

The Google Wallet app for iOS becomes the central hub for purchase management in agentic commerce through Gemini. In it, you can view active tasks to see which purchases Gemini is working on, as well as completed purchases and receipts.

Google has been working on two technologies to support its agentic commerce strategy: Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and Agent Payments Protocol (AP2).

UCP is a technical language that enables AI agents to communicate with retailers and make purchases, while AP2 is the payment framework that establishes rules and authorization for agents to make payments.

Google Wallet serves as both the AI-powered wallet and the consumer-facing record of transactions made by Gemini.

Also: Google Wallet has a lot of new tricks – these 5 are my favorites

Along with Google, major retailers supported the development of UCP, including Shopify, Walmart, Target, and Etsy. When Google announced AP2, more than 60 organizations became involved, including PayPal, Salesforce, Mastercard, and American Express.

#3036. How to Turn Off Apple Intelligence Feature by Feature in iOS 27

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Whether you want to drop a few AI features or as many as possible, here's where each control can be found in iOS 27.

iOS 26 lets you turn off Apple Intelligence with one toggle. iOS 27 doesn’t. Apple folded its AI settings into a new Siri menu centered on Siri AI and dropped the master switch along the way, so opting out now means working through several parts of Settings. Siri AI’s controls are in the Siri menu, Screen Time can block Writing Tools and image creation, notification summaries have their own switch and each app’s Siri & Search settings control what Siri learns from it. This guide walks through every step in order.

Individual features can still be disabled, but they’re scattered across several menus in Settings and Screen Time rather than being consolidated in one place. Here’s the current map of what can be turned off and where to find each control.

If your device is not running the newest software, turning off Apple Intelligence all at once only takes a few taps in Settings and doesn’t affect any core iPhone functionality. Here’s how to do it on iPhone, iPad and Mac.

You can still disable some of Apple’s AI features if your iPhone is running iOS 27. It just won’t be as easy as tapping the main toggle.

To disable Siri AI, go to Settings > Siri and toggle off the control. Beware, though, that this will disable your voice assistant entirely, as well as disable conversations in the new dedicated Siri app and block you from using Apple’s Visual Intelligence. Additionally, your HomePod speakers will not be able to recognize your voice or help with personal content if they’re on the same iCloud account as your iPhone.

Keep reading for how to disable some of the individual Apple AI features.

Since the first Apple Intelligence features rolled out in iOS 18.1, some people have opted out of the new technology. Tools such as Image Playground, Genmoji and message summaries can use up to 7GB of your device’s internal storage — a sizable chunk, especially if you tend to run against the upper limit of its free space.

Even if storage is not an issue, you just may not be interested in Apple’s set of AI features. A recent CNET survey finds that just 19% of US smartphone owners are choosing to upgrade their devices to take advantage of new AI features. And a recent ZDNET/Aberdeen survey reveals that the majority of US adults say they will not use most AI features, and just 8% would consider paying extra for them. Some AI features are more welcome than others, with 58% of respondents saying using AI for photo editing would be valuable.

Or, honestly, you may not want to deal with features that are creating inaccurate summaries or that can be replicated without Apple Intelligence.

(Earlier iOS 18 updates re-enabled Apple Intelligence automatically even if you had turned it off, but as of iOS 18.4, the setting is honored.)

Read more: Did a well-meaning friend send you a message about Apple Intelligence possibly reading your private information? Here’s what’s actually going on.

I’m not an AI crank — I appreciate features such as notification summaries and the Clean Up tool in the Photos app. And yet, Apple Intelligence is also a work in progress, an evolving set of features that Apple is heavily hyping while gradually developing. I wouldn’t hold it against you if you wanted to not be distracted or feel like you’re doing Apple’s testing for them (that’s what the developer and public betas should be for).

Remember that Apple Intelligence works only on the new iPhone 18 lineup, the iPhone Duo, iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, iPhone 17E, iPhone 16, iPhone 16E, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro or M-series Macs and iPads, plus the newest iPad mini.

If you’re concerned about the storage requirements of Apple Intelligence, you can find out how much the system is using by going to Settings > General > iPhone (or iPad) Storage > iOS (or iPadOS).

See how much space Apple Intelligence is using in Settings. This is what it looks like running iOS 26, but the settings flow is the same.

Note that even after turning off Apple Intelligence, the storage still shows up in the iOS Storage list. However, I was able to confirm that if the phone’s storage fills up and the system needs that now-inactive space, iOS reclaims what it needs.

Maybe you’re finding some Apple Intelligence features helpful while others are annoying (or just highly amusing). You can turn off specific features in the settings for apps to which they apply.

For example, to disable text summaries in Messages notifications, go to Settings > Apps > Messages and switch off the Summarize Messages option.

Some features are not as app-specific. Writing Tools, which use Apple Intelligence to proof or rewrite text, appear as an option when you select text, regardless of the app. To turn that off, you need to disable Apple Intelligence system-wide.

Also note that nearly every app includes an “Apple Intelligence & Siri” option in Settings, with a Learn from this App option (turned on by default). That applies just to whether Apple Intelligence and Siri can monitor how you use it to make suggestions; it doesn’t affect any particular Apple Intelligence features.

Another option for restricting what Apple Intelligence can do is buried in the Screen Time settings. Screen Time is designed to control which apps and features can run on another device, such as the iPhone used by a child in your household. But it’s also helpful for tracking how much time you’re spending on the device and, in this case, turning off some components of Apple Intelligence.

Turn off selected Apple Intelligence features in the Screen Time settings. This is what the settings look like with iOS 26. It may look different if you are using iOS 27. The settings flow is the same.

If you haven’t upgraded to iOS 27 yet, make a good backup first.

If you aren’t on iOS 27, you can turn off Apple Intelligence with one tap. (You can see what software your iPhone is running by going to Settings > General > About and seeing what iOS version you’re running.)

If you’re on iOS 26 or earlier, here’s how to disable Apple Intelligence. Open Settings (iPhone or iPad) or System Settings (Mac) and choose Apple Intelligence & Siri. Then turn off the Apple Intelligence option. Confirm your choice in the dialog that appears by tapping Turn Off Apple Intelligence.

Turn off Apple Intelligence entirely with one switch if you are running iOS 26 or an earlier software version.

Curiously, the Clean Up tool in Photos sticks around even when Apple Intelligence is turned off, perhaps because the first time you use it the app downloads resources for it and holds onto them.

#3035. Nvidia Is Down 31% From Its Peak. History Says This Happens Next

Nvidia rebounded incredibly the last time it saw a steep pullback.

By Harsh Chauhan – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:26PM EST

Shares of Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) reached a 52-week high on Oct. 6, but they have dropped by a remarkable 31% since then, as investors pressed the panic button for multiple reasons.

Co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's resignation (before he was reinstated on Nov. 23), an investigation into Nvidia's dealings in China, and a reported probe by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) into the company's accounting practices have sent the stock packing over the past month and a half. The negativity surrounding Nvidia stock was so severe that even its quarterly results and better-than-expected guidance didn't arrest its slide.

However, Nvidia rallied over 31% following Huang’s reappointment, suggesting that investor confidence in the stock could improve. What’s more, the last time Nvidia witnessed such a sharp pullback in a short period, it went on a multi-year rally. Let's take a look at what happened in 2018.

Nvidia stock fell 54% between October and December 2018. This massive slide was triggered by an oversupply in the graphics processing unit (GPU) market, driven by a drop in cryptocurrency-related sales. Additionally, the company was caught up in a broader sell-off of tech stocks at the time.

Nvidia's growth slowed as crypto-driven GPU demand faded, leaving the company with excess inventory. In fact, Nvidia's revenue in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2019 (which ended in January 2019) fell 24% year over year to $2.2 billion. The company's non-GAAP earnings dropped by 53% from the year-ago period during the quarter.

Investors decided to book profits in Nvidia stock following stellar returns in 2016 and 2017. Nvidia lost 31% of its value in 2018. For comparison, it jumped by 227% in 2016 and 82% in 2017. So, this isn't the first time that Nvidia stock has lost its wheels and undergone a significant correction in a short time.

However, what's worth noting is that Nvidia went on a stunning bull run starting in 2019, driven by multiple catalysts, including strong GPU sales during the novel coronavirus pandemic and the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) in late 2022. Nvidia stock has jumped by a whopping 4,740% since the beginning of 2019.

So, savvy investors who saw the long-term opportunity in Nvidia's shares at that time are sitting on massive gains right now, even after the stock's recent sell-off. What's more, a closer look at Nvidia's valuation suggests that it is way more attractive right now than it was in 2018.

Nvidia traded at less than 18 times earnings at the end of 2018. The stock currently has a price-to-earnings ratio of 17.7, close to the level it traded at eight years ago. The forward earnings multiple of just 10 suggests that Nvidia is on track to deliver healthy bottom-line growth.

Meanwhile, the stock's price/earnings-to-growth (PEG) ratio was just 0.31 at the end of 2018. This is a forward-looking valuation metric that's calculated by dividing a stock's trailing earnings multiple by the projected annual earnings per share (EPS) growth over the long run, let's say for five years. A PEG ratio below 1 means that the stock is undervalued when its growth potential is considered.

So, Nvidia was significantly undervalued at that time, just like it is right now. The stock currently has a PEG ratio of just 0.19, which means that investors are getting an even better deal than in 2018. But should they take this opportunity to buy shares given recent developments at the company?

Investors are most likely in a classic dilemma right now. Nvidia's valuation suggests that the stock is a screaming buy, especially given its solid fundamentals, healthy growth, and sunny prospects.

The company reported impressive year-over-year revenue growth of 103% in the third quarter of fiscal 2027 to $115.8 billion. Adjusted earnings per share shot up by 111% to $2.68. The numbers easily exceeded consensus EPS expectations of $2.48 and the $109.1 billion revenue estimate. The company expects $130 billion in revenue in the current quarter, a 91% jump over last year and well ahead of the $125.1 billion Wall Street estimate.

Notably, analysts have raised their EPS expectations for Nvidia, indicating continued confidence in the company's prospects.

NVDA EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

Even the 12-month median price target of $232 implies a 41% jump, according to CNN. So, investors with a higher risk appetite who have investable cash after paying their bills, clearing expensive loans, and saving for a rainy day can consider buying this semiconductor stock. That's because Nvidia could go on a massive bull run, fueled by Huang’s comeback and the solid growth that it is poised to deliver, which could lead the market to reward it with a higher valuation in the future.

After all, Nvidia sees tremendous opportunity in the AI infrastructure market, and it is making solid progress in emerging niches, such as physical AI. However, the ongoing regulatory troubles the company faces suggest it may be wise for conservative investors to wait on the sidelines.

#3033. 90% of employers reject resumes that look like AI – yet half use AI to interview

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

In today's job market, do applicants really have a choice of whether to comply with AI hiring tools?

Hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider. At the same time, they’re turning to AI to help screen more candidates — meaning those videos you’ve seen on the internet of people pranking AI interviewers aren’t going away anytime soon.

New data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost

“The survey data is self-reported, so it reflects what employers believe has happened, not a measured outcome,” Greenhouse’s Head of Voice AI Ophir Samson told ZDNET via email.

Employers are also reacting to AI by adjusting their hiring processes: 86% of those surveyed reported changes to account for AI’s impact. 57% of them did so by adding another human interview.

“As jobseekers rely more on AI to polish and send out their job applications, employers are finding it harder to tell who’s actually right for the role,” the report stated, echoing an ongoing push-and-pull between applicants and hiring teams. AI resume screeners automatically toss a majority of applications they deem unfit, so applicants try not to get tossed by formatting their material for the screener, which then backfires anyway.

The report shows how a tough economy and an influx of AI hiring tools are colliding, arguably to benefit employers over applicants. Greenhouse noted that, ironically, AI tools are helping hiring managers while also making resumes untrustworthy, and applicants would rather be interviewed by AI than not at all.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams

“A growing number of employers are using AI not just to filter candidates out, but to have conversations with more candidates, earlier, through AI-powered voice technology,” Greenhouse said, adding that “half now use AI interviews to hear from more candidates, and 40% of those have found strong candidates they would have missed.”

Greenhouse itself offers a voice AI screening interview tool. Samson told ZDNET that an HR professional ran 200 candidates she’d rejected through Greenhouse’s tool, and it suggested 19.

“All five of the finalists came from that group, and she ultimately hired one from the group,” Samson said.

What we don’t, and maybe can’t, know is the inverse: whether AI screeners influence hiring managers to turn away candidates they actually should have considered. At least in Greenhouse’s case, Samson said Voice AI doesn’t make hiring decisions or “automatically advance, reject, or rank candidates.”

“Recruiters review every output, and one recruiter owns the outcome and can explain how they reached it,” he said.

Greenhouse’s report surveyed 1,347 hiring managers and recruiters across the US, UK, Germany, Australia, and Ireland from late September to mid-October, and found that half of employers using voice AI “say the early-stage candidate experience has improved.”

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

It’s unclear what “improved” means there, though, and whether applicants themselves would agree with that. Still, when given the choice, only 7% of applicants in the US would turn down an AI interview, per an earlier Greenhouse report. Additionally, “70% of those who’ve had a live AI interview say it helped them show their skills,” that report said.

But how swayed is that by the state of the US job market? October’s job report was better than expected, but it’s still been a tough year overall for job-seekers. Greenhouse’s findings could be as much a reflection of how desperate applicants are as an endorsement of or comfort with AI screenings.

“The job market could be a factor. Our Future of Hiring Candidate Report shows 81% of job seekers were rejected from a job in the past year without speaking to anyone at the company, human or AI,” Samson said. “But I’d be careful about reading the data as desperation. Candidates are setting clear conditions: nearly half (49%) want to know if a human will review their responses and 40% want to know how they’ll be evaluated.”

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires – and 5 ways smart leaders generate real value instead

Samson said that a software engineer named Ryan Quinlan, who was hired at Blissway, initially thought “talking to an AI” sounded stranger, but that it ultimately “felt like a conversation” that let him mention skills he’d forgotten to include on his resume. Samson said that Ryan has been “a ‘maybe’ on paper,” but that the AI interview helped him get over the line to be considered.

“For most applicants, a human conversation was never on the table,” Samson said. “The real choice is a resume lost in a pile, or 15 minutes to tell their story.”

Greenhouse found that while employers are using AI to screen more candidates, most are maintaining human oversight over the most important decisions in the hiring process.

“Of all the tasks employers would hand to an AI agent, deciding which candidates to advance came last, at just 7%,” Greenhouse said.

A recent California law aims to protect employees from being fired by AI systems that make determinations about their performance without a human co-signing the assessment. As with many AI productivity tools in the workplace, proper adoption ideally equates to more time for human workers to handle more important tasks.

Also: 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside

“Of employers who’ve saved time with AI, 85% put it back into candidates, most often by spending more time with shortlisted candidates (45%) and interviewing more candidates earlier (40%),” Greenhouse said.

The main question around AI interviewers remains whether they’re correctly capturing your interview the way you’d hope a human interviewer would (though that’s still deeply subjective and out of applicants’ control anyway).

“When AI interviews are implemented thoughtfully and transparently, they pay off for both candidates and recruiters,” Samson said. “Every candidate who uses our Voice AI can opt out, and about 90% rate the experience as excellent.”

#3032. Everything Is Falling Apart, and AI’s Fingerprints Are Everywhere

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

AI is rewriting the web in its own imperfect image, making software flaws easier to find and easier to exploit, while introducing plenty of its own imperfections.

I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.

Microsoft Outlook? Broken, for a bit. Air traffic control? Had some issues. Bank with Chase? Monday was not great. But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto. I am almost certainly forgetting some.

Something must be behind all of this, you might think — a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet? But the answer is more complicated than that. All of these issues, and the ones that will happen after I write this, are probably unconnected, at least in the concrete sense. But they exist in a world where the infrastructure of the internet and the whole human world it undergirds looks increasingly precarious.

Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counteradversary operations at cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, called last month “Black October.” This month? “Blacker November.” December probably isn’t looking great.

“This is not getting better, unfortunately,” Meyers told me.

One big reason for all of this, although not the only one, is artificial intelligence, but maybe not in the ways you expect.

If it’s connected to the internet, it’s at risk. Websites, sure. But also utilities like power plants and water treatment facilities or, for some reason, grocery store freezers.

In the olden days, like six months ago, a hacker taking control would have required a fairly complicated set of skills, honed over a long career, perhaps in the employ of a government or criminal organization.

Artificial intelligence, especially models developed and released this year, has changed things. AI has “democratized” hacking, cybersecurity experts told me. Things that used to require the capabilities and focus of a team of people with a clear goal can be done by a 20-something with an AI model and a specially designed program around it. And you don’t have to be a big or valuable target anymore to be worthy of a hacker’s attention.

At the same time, AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities. These models and agents — essentially AI models that can do things on their own — can comb through websites or code and find problems that might have escaped the notice of humans. And they can do so more cheaply, meaning they can be turned on code that might not otherwise have gotten a close look. So many vulnerabilities are being exposed that it’s been given an appropriately bleak name: the vulnpocalypse.

Even that defensive advantage is a double-edged sword. Before, it might have taken weeks before a newly discovered vulnerability could be exploited. Now it might take days, even hours. If you’re responsible for a website or any of those things connected to the internet that may or may not still be maintained by their creators, you may not be paying attention and know you should update. You may find yourself liable if a breach leads to a leak of customer data. You may not have the know-how to fix it.

Another risk introduced by AI is that the technology, trained on all the lines of code its creators could find, is really good at writing code. Software engineers know this, and companies are now maintaining smaller teams of human engineers using AI to write more and more software. That code might be OK, but it might not be, and there’s a chance no human ever looked at it to be sure.

When I connected with John Strand over video chat, he was in Germany for a conference, and he was smiling. That wasn’t good. “You need to understand that whenever an offensive security person smiles and gets excited,” he said, “it’s bad.”

As owner and CEO of Black Hills Information Security, Strand’s job is to test systems for weaknesses, to think like an attacker and poke holes in a client’s defenses. He says he’d been getting a bit bored with the work after decades of the same techniques until the cyber capabilities of AI models started to explode at the end of 2025. New AI models were great at finding weaknesses in code, and AI agents could do the boring, time-consuming part.

“You’re seeing something that can automate the kind of grinding grunt work of offensive security and bring that to a human operator much faster,” Strand said.

Things have only accelerated since the summer. AI agents are capable of more autonomy. And attackers have better tools to refine the often blunt instruments of AI models — harnesses. While an AI model can do a lot of things, a harness provides the tools and direction that allow it to do a specific thing more effectively. Think Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI’s Codex, but for hacking. Perhaps the biggest, most notable harness used by hackers is Artex, a significant-enough threat that the FBI issued a warning.

In September and October, a hack of major South Korean banks led to the theft of personal information. Meyers says CrowdStrike determined the attacker was likely a 26-year-old in China using Artex. After asking AI how to do the attack, the hacker succeeded, then asked the AI how to sell the stolen data on Telegram.

“Anybody out there can now be a nation-state-level hacker just by using the tool,” Meyers said.

Despite efforts by major AI developers to limit who can access their biggest and most capable models, the hacking and exploit skills attackers need are within the means of models already in the hands of attackers. That includes open-weight models that hackers can run on their own hardware, away from the guardrails and peering eyes of AI companies and government agencies.

“The genie’s out of the bottle, and there’s no putting it back in,” said Gary Barlet, public sector chief technology officer at Illumio, a firm that specializes in ransomware and breach containment.

AI-powered hackers, whether they’re individual vibe-hackers or government-backed cyberwarfare units intent on damaging critical infrastructure, always have an advantage. They just have to be right once, as the saying goes. Defenders have to be right every time.

The good thing is that the defenders are using the same tools as the attackers. And sometimes they have a head start. Programs like Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, OpenAI’s Daybreak and Google’s Fairwind let cybersecurity experts and high-profile targets like banks and healthcare providers have early access to the most capable models from those developers, often with fewer limits on what the models can find. The goal is to get a jump on patching and fixing the easiest and riskiest problems.

It still might not be enough, and Big Tech leaders know it. In an October appearance at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he no longer thought we’d be able to “just patch all the bugs” and that the problem is one that “is still something that we have not, as organizational leaders or countries or individuals, taken seriously.”

And defenders may not have much of a lead in patching bugs anyway, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the New York Times Dealbook Summit. Previously, when patching a critical system, you might have a week to test it before pushing it to production. “Right now the patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild,” Nadella said. “That’s going to create instability.”

The PHP vulnerability widely reported in October — with an urgent notice from the PHP Foundation for website owners to patch — stemmed from work through Patch the Planet, part of OpenAI’s Daybreak.

That’s just one high-profile recent disclosure. But there has been an avalanche of them. The National Vulnerability Database has received more than 10,000 instances of common vulnerabilities and exposures so far in November, after more than 17,000 CVEs in October. For comparison, in October 2025, that figure was less than 5,000.

“There’s effectively this big backlog of security issues in the open-source world that hadn’t been discovered until AI was able to just spend tons of time analyzing it and finding these vulnerabilities,” said Matt Wyckhouse, CEO of Finite State, a cybersecurity company focused on connected devices.

It goes well beyond open-source software. The connected devices Wyckhouse focuses on include things like refrigerators and smart home gadgets — the kinds of things that probably didn’t have to be connected to the internet, but are. The source code of the firmware and software powering those products has been seen by far fewer eyes than something like PHP, an incredibly common coding language used by much of the internet. The code running these devices may not be on GitHub or floating around the internet, but an AI model might be able to reverse-engineer it and find an exploit. And suddenly an attacker can turn freezers into ovens. If you think ground beef is expensive now, imagine what would happen if a major retailer’s stock of hamburger all spoiled overnight.

“Refrigeration has to work for our society to function, as it turns out,” Wyckhouse said.

Wherever the vulnerability is found, it has to be patched. That’s where the backlog of issues is really wreaking havoc. Companies that create or just operate software are swamped with important, critical issues that have to be fixed now because it could only be hours before an attacker can exploit it. It’s why your computer and the software on it have to update so frequently these days.

“It’s daunting the amount of work and the amount of time it’s going to take to clean this whole thing up,” said Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov.

And patching isn’t perfect. Sometimes it’s not a cyberattack that causes a system to go down but the fix to prevent it. Software updates are believed to be responsible for several of the recent high-profile outages, including Apple’s issues on Tuesday.

Things get even hairier if the code isn’t great to begin with or presents new problems of its own. And with AI writing even more of it, that’s a growing issue.

In the backdrop of all of this chaos is the fact that software engineering is one of the industries most disrupted by AI. Models trained on miles of code are great at writing something that works — no matter how many holes are in it. And to CEOs eager to cut costs and boost their companies’ stock prices, the temptation is to lay off engineers and have fewer people use AI to do all that coding.

Big Tech has been laying off staff by the thousands this year. Microsoft’s October announcement that it was offering buyouts to 60,000 staff became a key talking point just weeks later when the system powering its Outlook email service went dark for a day. Might things break less often if more people were on hand to maintain them?

“I wouldn’t be surprised if companies start to backtrack on that more,” said Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at the database security firm Liquibase.

Companies might also have more junior developers writing and releasing code that would have previously gone through senior developers, with AI replacing the productivity, but not the experience, McCurdy says.

That means the problem isn’t just the vulnerabilities in existing software, but the vulnerabilities being written into new software or patches to existing software by AI. The same technology is causing the problem, providing the solution and complicating that solution.

The main thing we can do now is just… wait. Wyckhouse told me he thinks the next two years are going to be a period of growing pains as vulnerabilities are found and patched. The end result should be that everything is more stable.

“I think software is going to be an order of magnitude more secure by the end of the next year or two than it is today for this reason,” he said. “It will hurt a bit.”

Whether you’re an ordinary phone user or a major corporation, updating your software has become more important than ever.

“You’ve got to patch. You go for a flu shot, and you go and have your preventative healthcare,” Meyers said. “You need to do the same thing when it comes to cybersecurity.”

We don’t have to put up with it, Barlet says. “I think we need to start having higher expectations from the companies we’re consuming from,” he said.

#3031. What a $5,000 Investment in Shopify Stock Today Could Grow Into by 2030

The e-commerce business might more than double its cash flow per share by 2030. The stock's gain may be much lower.

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:43PM EST

Shopify (SHOP -1.48%) stock climbed around 9% on Monday, Nov. 23, closing at $134.30. Still, shares are down about 17% in 2026, and they'd have to rise about 33% to get back to the $179.22 record hit on Oct. 12.

The holiday shopping season, normally the e-commerce company's biggest stretch of the year, kicks off with Black Friday on Nov. 27.

At roughly $134 per share as I write, $5,000 buys about 37 shares. By my math, those shares might be worth about $6,800 at the end of 2030. That'd be a gain of about $1,800, or roughly 8% a year.

The estimate has Shopify's free cash flow per share more than doubling by 2030, even as growth cools. It also assumes investors will pay far less for every dollar of that cash flow than they do today, at about 65 times free cash flow.

After two straight quarters of 34% growth earlier in 2026, Shopify's revenue climbed 32% year over year in the third quarter, to around $3.7 billion. Management sees growth at a low-thirties percentage rate again in the fourth quarter, with gross profit growing at a high-twenties rate.

Free cash flow (the cash left after capital spending) has mostly kept pace with revenue, because Shopify's free cash flow margin hasn't changed much. Shopify kept 18% of its revenue as free cash flow in 2024 and 17% in 2025. Over the last four quarters, the number was around 19%, helped by a 22% third quarter. Management expects the fourth-quarter margin to match the 19% it reported a year before.

If fourth-quarter revenue rises around 31% at that margin, Shopify would finish 2026 with about $15.3 billion in revenue, up 32% from 2025, and about $2.9 billion in free cash flow, up around 40%. Spread over the third quarter's 1.29 billion diluted shares, that's around $2.20 of free cash flow per share.

The share count has been dropping, too. Shopify bought back around $2.5 billion of its stock in the first nine months of 2026, and its third-quarter diluted share count was down about 2% from a year earlier.

I've assumed revenue growth keeps slowing, from the low 30s now to the mid-teens by 2030, averaging about 20% a year from 2027 through 2030. That would put 2030 revenue around $32 billion, about twice this year's likely total.

If free cash flow holds just below 19% of revenue, where it should land in 2026, Shopify would produce almost $6 billion of it in 2030. And I've kept the share count near 1.29 billion, though buybacks have been lowering it. That puts 2030 free cash flow at around $4.60 per share, a little over twice this year's $2.20.

Shopify's market cap is about $173 billion at $134.30, putting the shares at about 65 times free cash flow. At its October record, Shopify fetched about 98 times free cash flow. And even at its lowest close in 2026, about $95 on May 13, it went for roughly 59 times free cash flow.

I've assumed 40 times free cash flow at the end of 2030. That's still a premium price, and it looks fair for a business that could be growing in the mid-teens by then. But it's far below anything investors have paid for Shopify this year.

At 40 times free cash flow, $4.60 per share gives a stock price around $184. Thirty-seven shares at that price are worth about $6,800.

Of course, another free cash flow multiple would change the result a lot. If investors still paid 65 times free cash flow in 2030, the $5,000 would grow to about $11,100. At 30 times free cash flow, it would be worth about $5,100, barely more than what went in.

Shopify's business looks healthy enough to keep growing its cash flow at an impressive rate. But my base case comes out to roughly 8% a year, and a less generous valuation in 2030 might erase most of that gain. This year alone, shares have closed as low as about $95 and as high as about $179.

With swings like that, I'd want a lower starting price before putting $5,000 into Shopify stock.

#3029. The Flipper One is more than a Zero 2.0 – it’s a $399 Linux computer with a $13M Kickstarter

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

Backers are going big on the $759 Ultimate Bundle, but Flipper warns that rising RAM prices could affect production.

The Flipper One crowdfunding campaign has broken the $13-million mark, smashing the funding raised for previous Flipper devices and demonstrating strong interest in the successor to the Flipper Zero. The $399 Flipper One is a pocket Linux computer focused on networking, with delivery estimated for July 2027. But it isn’t simply an updated version of the Flipper Zero. It’s a very different animal and a much more serious bit of kit.

The thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use. You could fire it up and turn the volume down on the TV at your parents’ place, see the radio waves coming from your car’s key fob, and copy hotel room key cards.

Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited

It could do a lot, there wasn’t a steep learning curve, and you didn’t need to buy anything else. Did the fake videos on TikTok from people claiming they could change the prices at gas stations (I wish!) or start cars remotely help make the Zero more popular?

Unfortunately, yes. But what made it successful was that it packed a lot of power into a package that was small, fun, affordable, and easy to use.

If the Flipper Zero, with its NFC, RFID, sub-GHz, and IR, was kindergarten, the Flipper One is a college degree: a pocket Linux computer focused on networking.

This is reflected in the price. You can pick up a Zero for $169, while the Flipper One is $399.

What this buys you is the Flipper One base computer with a 256 × 144 grayscale LCD, Rockchip RK3576 8-core ARM SoC with NPU, a low-power MCU for handling the LCD and user interface, 8GB of LPDDR5 RAM, 64GB of UFS 2.2 storage, and a microSD slot.

If that $399 feels like a lot, it’s worth keeping in mind that, according to Flipper, the price only covers production costs and that the RAM and UFS storage account for at least half of the total hardware cost.

If you think this is a lot, you could spend a lot more. Adding a LoRa, SDR, or 5G module will push the total up a lot higher. And if you want all three modules, you’re looking at $759 for the Flipper One Ultimate Bundle.

Also: The Flipper One is the Linux cyberdeck I wish my Raspberry Pi could be

The reception has been strong enough that pledges have flown past the $300,000 goal that Flipper initially set, with over 24,000 backers pledging over $13 million. Close to 5,300 backers have gone for the Ultimate Bundle, compared to just over 4,300 choosing the bare Flipper One.

This suggests that backers really want the radio capabilities that this new platform offers.

If you want one, this crowdfunding run is a good time to get one because it’s a Kickstarter Special slashing 25% off an estimated retail price of $550.

The response over on Reddit has been a little more subdued, with some being taken aback by the price of the Zero’s bigger sibling.

Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years

As someone who homebrews a lot of electronics, I’m going to say that the price is justified, and this project goes far beyond something you could put together with a Raspberry Pi and some code.

The Flipper One campaign runs until Dec. 17, 2026, with delivery estimated for July 2027.

Keep in mind that this is a Kickstarter pledge, not a purchase, and that rewards aren’t guaranteed. Flipper also says on the Kickstarter page that component shortages are the biggest risk to the project and that they “could cause significant delays to production and delivery.” It also says that if RAM prices continue to rise, it cannot “rule out adjusting some product specifications, including reducing the amount of RAM.”

Also: Is the Flipper Zero the best multi-tool for hacking?

And the good news here is that I’ve seen several analysts predicting that RAM prices will begin to go down in 2027 as demand eases off.

#3026. Your Google AI mode searches can stay private now with ‘temporary threads’ – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With temporary threads, any searches you run in Google’s AI Mode won’t be associated with your account or saved to your chat history.

Most of the major AIs offer a temporary chat or incognito option in which your conversation remains private and vanishes as soon as your chat ends. Now Google has jumped on board this bandwagon with its AI Mode searches.

Also: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI training

New to Google’s AI Mode is an option known as temporary threads. By choosing this setting, any searches you conduct in AI mode are detached from your own Google account and history. Your temporary searches won’t be affected by your past preferences or chats. They won’t be impacted by any personalization you’ve set up through your account. And they won’t be saved to your chat history. The goal here is to prevent anyone else, including Google, from accessing your conversations in this mode.

This option is currently rolling out around the world in all languages to Google search on both desktop and mobile browsers. You can run a temporary thread on any device and in any browser.

Try this for yourself: Head to the regular Google search page and click the button on the search field for AI Mode. You should then see an icon with a pen hovering over a dotted circle. If you don’t see it, you may have to run a search to get started. On the results page, you should then spot the icon.

Hover over the icon, and the tooltip will say: “Start temporary thread.” Click the icon on the left to start a new thread. Now, any conversation you kick off will be temporary and unconnected to your account. But you don’t have to stick with just plain old text. Select the plus icon to upload an image or file. Select the microphone icon to speak instead of type.

Also: Goodbye, Gemini Gems: How to use Google’s new Skills

Certain limitations are in effect with a temporary thread. Specifically, you can’t do any of the following:

Are these temporary threads truly private? Here’s what Google says:

“Temporary threads will not be saved to your Google account and disappear after 24 hours,” Google said on a support page. “They won’t be used to train Google’s generative AI models, unless you submit feedback or it’s necessary for safety purposes. Google will still collect data and use data that is not associated with your account, including to keep our services working smoothly and safely and to support business operations.”

Google also warns that your browser may still save your history if you visit a website within a temporary thread. Data could still be collected by the sites you visit and the services those sites use, including Google services like Google Analytics.

Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes

ChatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot all offer a temporary chat mode that also promises to keep your chats private and unconnected to your account. Claude and Perplexity provide the same feature but call it incognito mode.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3025. Can an App Tell When Someone Near You Is Wearing Smart Glasses?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Apps such as Zuckoff scan for the Bluetooth signals smart glasses send out, giving bystanders a way to know a pair is nearby.

Meta’s smart glasses stay connected to the wearer’s phone over Bluetooth, and that connection is what detector apps look for. Apps such as Zuckoff scan for the short broadcast signals Bluetooth devices send out and compare them with signals from known smart glasses models. When there’s a match, the app sends an alert. It’s a practical way to learn that a pair is nearby, though the alert can’t confirm whether anyone’s recording, and glasses with Bluetooth switched off won’t appear at all. Here’s how the apps work and how much weight to give an alert.

It’s a clever workaround for glasses designed to blend in. How useful it is depends on what you want it to tell you: The app can detect that a pair is close by, but not whether it’s recording. Still, that’s more notice than most people get today, especially if they haven’t spotted the glasses’ built-in LED indicator.

Here’s how those apps work, what they reliably catch and what they miss.

Zuckoff, whose name takes a direct jab at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, has joined a small ecosystem of apps such as Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner and Nearby Glasses that offer similar functionality — letting you know when someone has smart glasses activated and how close the device is, although they can’t tell you specifically whether someone is actively recording or using AI to pull up information. The apps detect approximate device proximity by sweeping local Bluetooth frequencies to locate vendor IDs, system identifiers and hardware signatures associated with smart glasses.

As Zuckoff’s website notes: “Glasses advertise loudest while powering on, pairing or leaving the case. Once paired to their owner’s phone, they can go quiet, so silence is not proof that nobody is recording, and a detection is not proof that anyone is. Signal strength gives a rough distance and no direction at all.”

Zuckoff’s developer, Pawel Szydlowski, said he was already working on projects that used Bluetooth to detect nearby devices and discovered the tech could be applied to smart glasses. “It’s just the same technology wrapped in a different paper,” he said in a video chat with CNET.

Recent reports have shown that smart glasses are being used for everything from bullying in schools to viral videos with unwitting subjects who don’t know they’re being recorded.

Since it launched in early August, the Zuckoff app has gotten 2,000 sign-ups, and Szydlowski is beta-testing an Android version he hopes to make available on the Google Play Store. The app also has a premium version for $10 a year that can run continuous detection checks in the background when the app isn’t in use.

But a booming ecosystem of DIY modifications and third-party hardware hacks is also giving smart glasses wearers unprecedented stealth by allowing them to disable the activation lights, either by bypassing the capture LEDs or by patching software to suppress system notifications.

Tech journalist Joanna Stern hosted a video showing the process in which a local hacker removed the LED light from her Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $100, allowing the wearables to secretly record without notice.

Detecting active smart glasses in public or private spaces adds a new layer of security awareness, but it raises an obvious dilemma: What do you actually do with that information? Once a detector app alerts us that smart glasses are nearby, it seems our only choices are to either leave the space or ask the wearer to remove the glasses.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington who studies the societal impacts of technology, says we’re still figuring out the social norms around wearables like smart glasses. It’s impossible to know whether the person filming will behave responsibly, and the question of consent gets even thornier if children might be captured on video or in photos.

“Until we develop clear mechanisms to balance seamless innovation with consent, these devices will continue to turn everyday public spaces into zones of surveillance anxiety,” she said.

The Even G2 smart glasses don’t have a camera for recording photos or videos. They can pair with a separately sold R1 control ring that works as a fitness tracker.

For instance, Even Realities’ G2 smart glasses don’t include a front-facing camera at all. Instead, the Even G2 devices, released in late 2025, focus on providing the wearer with information and acting more like a personal assistant.

“We made the decision from the beginning that smart glasses don’t need to have cameras on them in order to be useful,” Even Realities CEO Will Wang told CNET in an email. “We believe something worn on your face should respect not only the person wearing it, but everyone around them.”

The G2 devices don’t record externally, a design choice Wang said gave the company a unique challenge. “Leaving the camera out also pushed us to think differently about what actually makes smart glasses useful day to day, rather than assuming more sensors automatically make a better product,” he said.

Wang said there’s room in the smart glasses market for different approaches to features and functionality, and that buyers may want to make trade-offs for devices they’ll wear on their faces. But Wang noted that the rise of smart glasses detectors indicates that social acceptance is an issue the industry needs to consider.

Over the last several months, smart glasses have been getting cheaper. And with more models and companies jumping into the fray, the demand for surveillance detectors is likely to grow — that is, unless Big Tech and wearable companies radically change their devices to make them invisible to detector apps.

Szydlowski said his hope is that, in time, Zuckoff won’t be needed at all. He pointed out that the ability to detect nearby Apple AirTag devices eventually became part of the operating systems on iOS and Android devices. If consumers pressure manufacturers and their governments to make smart glasses easier to detect, it would be “the perfect solution” to make his app obsolete, he said.

#3023. I’ve tested countless Linux distros, and Pond is unlike anything I’ve tried – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

Feeling adventurous? This Linux distribution is exciting, efficient and totally unique.

Linux is all about choice. From the kernel all the way up to the desktop environment, you get to determine what is used and even how it is used. The staggering number of distributions, desktops, package managers, file managers, and terminal apps provide you with a nearly infinite combination of choices. That choice is and has always been a key aspect of Linux.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me

So too is innovation. If there’s one thing that separates Linux from all other operating systems, it’s the willingness to try something different. Linux developers are always pushing the limits of what an operating system is, and this new take on the OS is the epitome of that.

The distribution in question is called Pond. According to the developers, “Pond is an opportunity for us to play with familiar conventions and experiment with new ideas that make a computer more natural and satisfying.”

The developers have achieved something special. Pond takes the standard UI and turns it on its head. Part tiling window manager, part mobile UI, part GNOME, and part something we’ve never before seen, this desktop environment is special. It took me all of five minutes to fall in love with what they’ve created.

Also: The only 4 Linux email clients I recommend

If you’ve ever considered using a tiling window manager, but thought the lack of a mouse made it seem a bit too complicated, Pond is exactly what you want. Here’s how it works:

Pond uses the Niri window manager to arrange windows in columns along an infinite strip from left to right. In multi-monitor setups, each display gets its own strip, so windows never “overflow” from one monitor to the next.

Also: How to install Arch Linux without losing your mind

At the same time, workspaces are dynamic, and there’s always a new workspace automatically created to the right of the farthest-right window. The combination of the Pond sidebar and Niri’s way of handling windows makes this UI truly original.

Pond doesn’t have a traditional desktop menu. Instead, you open the launcher (using the Super+Space key combination), type the name of the app you want to install, and hit Enter when the app name appears on both the display and as an icon in the top portion of the sidebar.

Another thing that sets Pond apart is how you install apps. Yes, you can open a terminal window and install an app using the pacman command, or you can open the launcher, type install, press Enter, and then type the name of the app you want to install. For instance, if you wanted to install LibreOffice, you would type:

Once you hit Enter a second time, the installation will begin. Many apps install via Flatpak, but on the off-chance an app must be installed via the pacman package manager, you’ll be prompted to type your user password before the installation begins.

As I hinted earlier, Pond is based on Arch Linux, which means it’s a rolling-release distribution. One issue that did give me pause was the lack of a GUI update system, which indicates that updates would have to happen in the terminal, like so:

I installed the Shelly GUI frontend, which does have an update component. Personally, I would simply open the terminal window, type sudo pacman -Syu, hit Enter, and let the update run in the background. But if a GUI is your jam, Shelly is what you want.

Also: A super fast distro for anyone ready to move beyond beginner Linux

It would be sweet if the developers allowed updating the system from within the launcher, so it didn’t require opening the terminal first. The Pond launcher does allow running system commands from the launcher, which will then open the terminal window and execute the command. For instance, open the terminal, type a command, hit Enter, and then scroll through the list of available commands that can be run.

Pond ships with kernel 7.3.4-3, so it has outstanding hardware recognition and performance.

You should definitely give Pond a try, especially if you’re adventurous and want to experience something completely different. If, on the other hand, different is not in your stream, then Pond will frustrate you to no end.

Also: Why Nextcloud Office is my new favorite free productivity suite

Pond excited me more than any OS has in a very long time; so much so that I could see this becoming my go-to OS, once it reaches stable release. Until then, I will keep Pond installed on a laptop, keep upgrading, and see what happens next.

Kudos to the Pond OS team for coming up with something truly unique in an already competitive world.

#3022. Nothing’s AI Earbuds Will Serve as an All-in-One Conversation Recorder

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

While most AI-powered peripherals record only phone calls or in-person chats, the Ear Note is designed to capture every conversation.

Phone-maker Nothing Technology is breaking away from its typical retro-inspired designs with a new pair of AI-powered earbuds, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The company confirmed via an X post that its Ear Note wireless earbuds will be available starting Dec. 8.

The Ear Note earbuds are designed primarily to maximize the recording functionality. While other AI earbuds have already hit the market, the Ear Note is the first to record both phone calls and in-person conversations.

Nothing shared that the Ear Note will work with multiple popular AI agents, but the full list of compatible software has not yet been released. The Ear Note works in tandem with an app that stores recordings from the earbuds and case, creating transcriptions and summaries similar to those created by the popular Otter AI app.

The Nothing brand has developed a cult following for combining lifestyle and fashion trends in its suite of smartphones, headphones, speakers and watches.

The full product lineup is built with modern hardware, but mimics warm, nearly retrofuturist design sensibilities. The blocky Ear Note charging case continues this trend while taking the company’s tech in a new direction.

In the lead-up to the Ear Note’s reveal, Nothing CEO Carl Pei described the earbuds in an X post as “a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.”

In a Bloomberg interview, Pei indicated that Nothing isn’t trying to create AI agents or software, but that the company has a “really interesting opportunity to be the hardware layer to AI.”

It’s currently unclear how much the Ear Note earbuds and case will cost when they’re released next month. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the company hasn’t settled on a price just yet. The most expensive earbuds currently available on the Nothing store cost $149.

Whether you’re covering your eyes, plugging your ears or slapping a timepiece on your wrist, there’s now an ever-present option to record the world around you. Multiple companies have created their own versions of smart glasses, earbuds and watches with augmented reality capabilities.

Now that AI is the flavor du jour, these existing features are being enhanced by new ways to scan and interact with the surrounding environment. That means a lot of visual and auditory data is being recorded by wearable devices, and very rarely with the consent of all parties involved.

The most immediate risk factors are associated with video recording – public distrust of smart glasses is so widespread that they’ve colloquially been coined “pervert glasses,” as folks fear they fundamentally break an unspoken social contract by obscuring public recording from other people.

But audio recording, enabled by Apple’s latest smartwatches, the Amazon Bee, Plaud earbuds and the new Ear Note, is also raising concerns, not least because many states require all-party consent before you can record conversations.

The Ear Note’s ability to record every bit of audio, from phone calls to in-person conversations, means it will be handling more sensitive information than other AI-powered earbuds. The company will need to face new challenges to ensure security measures are in place to prevent private chats from leaking.

Pei called wearables with recording functionality a sensitive space, and said the design team was “extra careful to not take any risks.” The Ear Note earbuds and case are largely controlled by user commands, including tactile button presses that begin the recording process.

#3021. Meta Muse booked an Airbnb without permission – and that’s not the worst of it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse said the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize.

These incidents “prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data,” Reuters said.

Reuters said “an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: ‘BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2,722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5,899.57.'” In another instance, Muse booked a non-refundable Airbnb for an employee who hadn’t instructed it to.

Muse notified another employee, who was using the agent on her personal phone, about a message she’d received on Signal, though she said she hadn’t given the agent access to the encrypted messaging app.

Reuters and the AI Now Institute determined, through testing on an Android phone and a Mac, that Muse used “permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.” Because Muse is set up with automatic access to Android push notifications, it didn’t need explicit app access to read messages.

The tests did not work on an iPhone, suggesting better protections against Muse’s prying.

Similarly, in September, a user reported Muse had shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before checking with him. The incident was ultimately a misunderstanding between the terms the user thought he’d consented to and how much access he was actually handing over, which exemplifies that Meta and the user may have explicitly different definitions of access, and that Muse can take advantage of that grey area.

Meta told Reuters these incidents were either isolated or the result of hallucinations, though Reuters could not confirm that.
