#2985. Jensen Huang's Return Could Make a Tesla/SpaceX Merger More Likely

The regulatory environment looks more forgiving after Huang's return.

By Jeremy Bowman – Nov 24, 2026 at 9:30PM EST

Tesla (TSLA -0.20%) and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -5.65%), Elon Musk's two trillion-dollar companies, took a step closer to merging on Tuesday.

Both companies have appointed a total of five directors, three from Tesla and two from SpaceX, to guide two special committees to handle merger negotiations.

The committees have also hired investment banks to develop financial models for the all-stock merger, and a deal could be reached before year's end. If the merger were timely enough, it would also allow SpaceX to be included in the S&P 500 earlier than it would as a stand-alone company.

Naturally, merging two companies that have the same CEO is easier than merging two unrelated companies. Musk has a majority of SpaceX's voting power and 20% of Tesla's voting power, and could own a majority of the combined company.

The full details of Huang's return to Nvidia may never be clear, but President Trump says he played an active role in getting Huang reinstated, telling CNBC that he "convinced" the board to do so.

That move may have shifted the Overton window significantly in corporate governance, or what's considered acceptable, and also shows that Trump is willing to put his thumb on the scale for his corporate friends, at least when he believes it's in the country's interest, one of which is Musk.

The dynamics of getting the merger approved versus reinstating Huang are much different, however. Trump just needed to get the board's approval to get Huang back as Nvidia CEO. The Tesla/SpaceX merger, on the other hand, will face a battery of regulatory hurdles to get cleared.

China would be an issue in the merger, as Tesla has a significant business there, and SpaceX's technology would likely raise national security concerns. It would have to pass antitrust muster in both the U.S. and Europe, where there could be resistance to creating a company with a leading position across so many disparate industries. Additionally, Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson has expressed skepticism about corporate concentration and could challenge the combination.

Still, expectations of corporate governance and President Trump's own ability to influence such decisions have shifted with Huang's reinstatement, which could help the merger go through.

While the two companies haven't formally declared an intention to merge, they're likely to go through with it, as all of the interested parties, including Elon Musk, appear to be incentivized by a merger. The deal will serve as a major test for the regulatory apparatus, as antitrust regulators have blocked much smaller deals in the past.

#2983. An Unsecured Database Exposed About 2 Billion Login Records

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Cybersecurity

The files included passwords and data that can keep you signed in. The number of people affected is unknown.

A database containing about 2 billion login records for sites across the internet was accessible online without a password, security researcher Jeremiah Fowler said in a report published Tuesday by ExpressVPN. The collection included usernames and passwords tied to email, social media, shopping and financial services. Among the files was an ad offering access to email accounts sorted by geography.

The 2 billion figure is an estimate and not representative of the number of people affected, since some accounts may appear more than once and one person can have dozens of logins saved on a single device. Fowler reported the database to its hosting provider, which restricted public access several days later. It’s unclear how long the files had been exposed or who else may have accessed them.

Fowler’s estimate of about 2 billion login records applies to the database he found. Wired put the total at more than 3.5 billion by including a separate database that security firm UpGuard disclosed last week. That database held about 1.64 billion records, including Chinese national ID numbers, phone numbers and school enrollment records.

Some of the files Fowler reviewed appeared to be from infostealers — malicious software that collects saved passwords and other data from infected devices. Once that information is collected, brokers can buy it in bulk, sort it by country or account type and resell it in smaller batches. A buyer interested in email accounts in a particular country can pay for that slice of the data. The people selling it can make money from the same records more than once.

Fowler saw signs that the files came from multiple sources, but couldn’t determine who assembled the collection or whether it was used for sales, research or another purpose.

I saw a version of that business in my reporting on the dark web for CNET. On Genesis Market, buyers could shop for stolen accounts by location and category, including banking, email and social media. By the time authorities disrupted the marketplace in 2023, it had offered access to data from more than 1.5 million compromised computers, according to the Justice Department.

You can look up your email address in Have I Been Pwned to see whether it appears in a known data exposure. A clean result only tells you what’s in the service’s index.

If you see an unfamiliar login or suspect your device is infected, use a different, trusted device to change the affected password and sign out of other sessions. Start with your email if several accounts may be affected, since that’s where password reset links often go. Replace reused passwords with unique ones, use a password manager to keep track of them and turn on two-factor authentication where it’s available.

Identity theft protection services monitor for signs that your personal information has been exposed or misused. In a leak like this one, an alert about an exposed password can tell you which account to secure, especially if you’ve reused that password elsewhere. Aura is one of the services we tested for CNET’s guide to the best identity theft protection services.

#2981. World's Best Space Company SpaceX Will Soon Be 40% Better

Fresh off Starship Flight 15, Elon Musk promises a Starship 40% bigger -- and with 3x as many engines.

By Rich Smith – Nov 24, 2026 at 10:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

Any way you define it, I consider Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -5.65%) the world's best space company. SpaceX offers the lowest cost to orbit of any space company -- $74 million for 22.8 metric tons -- or about $3,245 per kilo to low earth orbit.

SpaceX launches more frequently than any other space company, too -- 161 times last year versus 21 for Rocket Lab, (RKLB -7.35%), America's second-most frequent launcher (and a launcher of much smaller rockets).

SpaceX has the world's biggest rocket in continuous operation, the Falcon Heavy, with a maximum payload approaching 64 tons, and will soon have an even bigger rocket in rotation -- Starship -- boasting a 100-ton payload.

Hard on the heels of Starship's partly successful Flight 15, which featured the first-ever tower capture of the spacecraft by Mechazilla after a return to space, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk announced plans to move ahead with an upgrade to Starship. Plans include a 40% increase in the spacecraft's size, which implies a 40% increase in payload to 140 tons and/or a 60% increase in the amount of fuel Starship can carry -- increasing its range and potentially putting the moon within reach.

SpaceX will also triple the number of Raptor engines on board the spacecraft to nine -- and upgrade their performance.

Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load. Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher thrust V4 engines.

Space watchers estimate that the latest version of Starship is protected by a total of 18,500 heat shield tiles, which protect the ship as it travels through the atmosphere during reentry. Lose too many of those tiles, and Starship probably blows up. Damage too many of those tiles, and it may take so long to replace them and refurbish the ship that it becomes no longer really "reusable," and more like "recyclable."

Which is why this next news is so important.

According to multiple space accounts I follow that have examined the condition of Starship after its Flight 15, only one heat shield tile appears to have sustained significant damage during reentry. That's a failure rate of just five one-thousandths of one percent (0.005%). And it implies that SpaceX will be both easier and cheaper to refurbish for reuse than previously hoped.

Musk himself confirmed this in a later post on X, suggesting reflight of a Starship could take as little as "a few weeks" as currently designed. And SpaceX's ultimate goal is still to tweak the design until it guarantees "zero expected refurbishment" and "immediate reusability (like an airplane)."

Yeah, I was going over the whole Starship heat shield earlier today. Overall, it looks great. The engines look great too. Ship 42 could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment. However, many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane), which requires zero expected refurbishment, apart from scheduled maintenance.

So what does all this mean to SpaceX shareholders?

Based on published (and rumored) payload capacities and launch prices, SpaceX's Falcon 9 is currently the cheapest non-government-owned rocket in the world.

Blue Origin's New Glenn, with low operating costs and a massive 45-ton payload, might challenge Falcon if Blue can get it operating consistently. But even if it achieves that goal, Starship is blazing a trail toward $1,000-per-kilogram prices for low earth orbit. A working Starship that costs $10 million to operate and charges $100 million per 100-ton launch would cost barely one-third of Falcon's per-kilogram price -- and half that of New Glenn.

It would generate roughly 90% profit margins for SpaceX (versus negative margins today, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence).

And it will be even more profitable if SpaceX makes it 40% larger.

I've said it before, and I'll say it again: advantage SpaceX.

#2980. Tidal to Reject and Remove Music That Is 100% AI

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The streaming app says it’s being flooded with AI-generated tracks.

The flood is too much for Tidal. The music streaming app announced on Tuesday that it is banning all tracks it determines to be entirely AI-generated. The platform said it’s making the move after being increasingly inundated with non-human music. As of Dec. 9, Tidal will no longer accept or host fully AI-generated tracks.

The app also said distributors, such as DistroKid, TuneCore, CD Baby and others, would not be allowed to deliver wholly AI-generated music.

According to Tidal, 43% of tracks distributed to the app over the past three months were completely AI-generated, including 60% of the music submitted on Nov. 6 alone. Tidal said the affected tracks were labeled as AI and removed from the royalty pool, which is the pot of subscription and ad revenue paid out to rights holders.

Before Tuesday’s action, Tidal had tried to lessen AI’s influence by identifying, labeling and demonetizing AI tracks, as outlined in its AI policy. But amid the growing influx of AI music, representatives for the app said it was time for “a more drastic change.”

Tidal said there are 27 million tracks in its catalog that are 100% AI, but 96% of them have not been streamed at all in the past three months. Those 27 million tracks make up 6.3% of Tidal’s entire listings.

The company has removed more than 65,000 tracks flagged for artist-name impersonation.

Some AI help is permitted. Musical tracks where the maker used AI assistance but did not rely on it to generate the entire track will be allowed on the platform. Tidal uses ⁠Ircam Amplify to detect AI.

Tidal didn’t specify how much AI help would be allowed.

A representative for Tidal didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Read more: I Only Listened to AI Music for a Week. It Was Terrible, but Not for the Reason You Think

“Tidal will always fight for artists to get paid more,” the company said in its announcement. “Everything in this update comes back to that. If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for or copied by someone pretending to be you.”

Generating music with AI is increasingly easy with online tools. The AI song-generation platform Suno can create songs using only text prompts. With Google’s Lyria, you can use photos or text prompts to generate tracks up to 3 minutes long.

It’s not illegal to create AI music and distribute it to streaming apps. Creators can’t legally clone the voice or likeness of real artists, nor can they violate copyright laws by copying the same lyrics and melodies. Creators also must follow the terms of service of the various streaming apps they distribute to.

AI music also is not just about creating hit songs. Some industries need affordable music for short-form videos, games, apps and retail spaces, and they are increasingly turning to AI to supply it.

But streaming apps and other companies are fighting back against AI slop, which refers to often poor-quality AI-generated social media posts, articles, music, videos and images inundating the internet in an attempt to generate click-and-stream revenue.

YouTube recently rolled out a new labeling system to indicate which music is AI-generated. Deezer provides a free tool listeners can use to see which tracks are AI-generated. Spotify is labeling which musicians are AI and which are human. Apple is flagging AI-generated music so listeners can spot it.

#2979. Nvidia Is Also Trying to Fix the Bug Causing Excessive SSD Writing

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Computing > Computer Accessories > Components > Graphic cards

Nvidia has issued software updates, but it's unclear if the problem is completely fixed.

Nvidia has had its share of drama lately, with the ousting and sudden un-ousting of CEO Jensen Huang after it was discovered he’d had multiple affairs, including one that involved an alleged member of a Chinese spy network. The fallout from the revelations was so significant that some worried Huang’s fate could be a major disruptor to the health of international markets and the future of the entire AI industry.

Given that, the world’s largest semiconductor company possibly wishes its biggest problem were software-related. But that won’t be much comfort to PC users affected by a software bug in Nvidia’s graphics driver that has caused some to experience excessive writes to their solid-state drives.

The issue began popping up in mid-November as posts on Nvidia’s support forums, as well as on Reddit and sites like HardForum, reported seeing as much as 30GB to 70GB of data per hour written to their SSDs. These types of drives wear down quickly over months of such use.

Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment and hasn’t made any public statements on the issue, but did acknowledge it in a hotfix and subsequent software update for its Windows 11 GeForce Game Ready Driver 621.40, where it said under Fixed General Bugs, “Excessive writes to file nvlog.nvlgstg may occur in background.” The driver that appeared to have caused the problems was released on Nov. 12.Some tech experts on social media had been suggesting rolling back to older graphics drivers before the hotfixes were released and warned that letting the problem go unchecked could cause an SSD to eventually fail.

Described by WCCF Tech as “a hotfix for the hotfix,” the new update appears to fix the issue in ways that the previous fix did not.

Nvidia’s software problem closely mirrors an issue AMD had with its own Adrenalin Edition graphics software just weeks ago. As of Nov. 18, AMD was still making tweaks to its graphics software to iron out any lingering problems.

PCGamer offered a way to check if your PC is affected by the excess writing issue.

Open Task Manager, click on the Details tab and right-click on the columns at the top to select “I/O write bytes” as one of your Task Manager columns. By doing that, you can see if the file “NVDisplay.Container.exe” is writing a huge amount of data to your data drive.

If that’s the case, you should update immediately to Nvidia’s latest drivers for the fix. In fact, it might be a good idea to update whether you’re experiencing high write rates or not, just to be safe.

#2978. Dell (DELL) Q3 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Infrastructure demand keeps pushing Dell's results to record levels this quarter.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 10:53PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Dell Technologies (DELL -11.83%) reported record quarterly results, with management stating that the company has transformed into an infrastructure-led organization where the Infrastructure Solutions Group drives the majority of revenue and profit. The company indicated that its expansion into AI-optimized servers has fundamentally shifted its financial profile, as evidenced by a $132.3 billion backlog and a 17% operating margin in its infrastructure business. Management reported that internal modernization efforts and the deployment of agentic AI have reduced operating expenses to 7% of revenue, the lowest level in the company's 42-year history. Strategic focus remains on meeting global demand for high-density compute, liquid-cooled data center architectures, and sovereign AI projects while maintaining a disciplined capital allocation framework through expanded share repurchases.

Any rebroadcast of this information in whole or part without prior written permission of Dell Technologies is prohibited. The presentation includes additional content that complements today's discussion. During this call, we'll refer to non-GAAP financial measures unless we say otherwise. And you can find reconciliations to the most comparable GAAP measures in our press release and presentation. Growth rates are on a year-over-year basis, unless otherwise noted. We'll also make forward-looking statements based on our current expectations. These statements speak only as of today, and actual results could differ materially because of risks and uncertainties described in our presentation and SEC filings, including our most recent Form 10-K and Form 10-Q.

We assume no obligation to update them. Now I'll turn it over to Jeff.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Thanks, Paul, and thanks, everyone, for joining us. I am proud of how our team performed, delivering another record quarter with strong execution and growth across the business. Revenue was a record $54.9 billion, up 103%. Diluted earnings per share was a record $9.45, up 265%. We generated $4.5 billion of cash flow from operations and returned a record $4.9 billion to shareholders. Our proven operating model, competitive advantages, speed to market and ability to drive scale are all delivering compounding benefits. Our modernization efforts are driving significant operating leverage. Operating expenses were 7% of revenue, the lowest in our company's 42-year history.

ISG, our most profitable business, has grown significantly over the past several years and drives the vast majority of our growth and profit. In fiscal '24, the year we began selling AI servers, ISG generated 38% of our revenue. Over the last 4 quarters, that contribution has increased to 68%. The trend is even more pronounced within operating income, where ISG's contribution has gone from 54% to 83%, and I expect the trend to continue into our next fiscal year. Over the same period of time, ISG's operating income rate expanded 2 points.

We achieved that expansion despite the tremendous growth in AI servers, supported by strong growth in Dell IP storage, the insatiable demand for compute and the efficiencies generated by our modernization efforts. Technology is driving material business outcomes and the demand for AI infrastructure and data center modernization remains strong. As AI infrastructure becomes more complex, our competitive advantage strengthen and our momentum accelerates. Our engineering and design capabilities are differentiated. We develop purpose-built bespoke solutions optimized for each customer's specific requirements, often working through many design iterations that contemplate not just the infrastructure, but the data center as a whole, designed for power, cooling, efficiency and software.

Our technical teams are leveraging AI and the proprietary knowledge we've built over the last 13 quarters to streamline and accelerate the design work, allowing our engineers to deliver complex designs in hours and quickly work through a large number of iterations. Our procurement capabilities and world-class supply chain are differentiated, especially in today's constrained supply environment. In manufacturing, we fully test the complete solution at L11 and beyond, including full rack power up, thermal compliance and scale-out and scale-up network validation before anything ships. Our deployment services team can stand up a rack within 6 hours of delivery. Our on-site support services help customers achieve 99-plus percent utilization with fewer spares than our competitors.

Together, these capabilities get infrastructure live faster. On large deployments, we can deliver time to first token 4 to 6 weeks faster than competitors while providing industry-leading total cost of ownership. That allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably. And of course, innovation remains central to our advantage. In Q3, we were the first OEM to ship a fully liquid cooled networking rack, extending our first-to-market leadership. We are now the only OEM shipping DLC 100% scalable units across compute, accelerators and networking with a standard L11 rack design, and we will be shipping storage liquid-cooled L11 racks in the near future.

The proof point is in our order momentum, $180 billion over the past 4 quarters, with a majority of our new orders based on NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72. We also led the industry with the launch of our AMD-based PowerEdge R9815 and R9825 platforms, delivering 238 world records in industry benchmarks in the R9825 alone. At the same time, AI technology continues to advance rapidly. Models have progressed from one-shot responses to reasoning to recursive capabilities and now agentic systems that act, manage and orchestrate workloads. As customer zero, we are moving from using AI as a tool and an adviser to using AI as an operator.

The first wave of AI answered questions and delivering productivity improvements of 10% to 40%. In the use cases, we are seeing agents drive productivity improvements an order of magnitude better, 10x or more by accelerating work and putting intelligence directly in front of decision-makers. Realizing those outcomes starts with strong leadership. Companies must simplify, standardize, automate processes before digitizing them or augmenting them with intelligence. They must also modernize their data architectures, including semantic data layers that provide context around their data and intellectual property. Agents generate significant token demand, increasing the need for modern, disaggregated infrastructure across AI and traditional servers, Dell IP storage, data management solutions and networking.

While enterprise traction is accelerating, the vast majority of customers remain in proof-of-concept and tool adoption phase. The broader agentic adoption opportunity is still ahead of us. Overall, AI and the quest for intelligence is expanding our TAM across our portfolio. This is no longer simply about IT budgets. Data centers are becoming value centers, driving growth, productivity, speed and intelligence across the enterprise. Now let's start with the results. Starting with ISG. Revenue increased 198% to a record $42 billion. Operating income was $7.1 billion, with an operating income rate of 17%. In AI servers, demand continues to accelerate. In Q3, we booked $60.2 billion in AI orders and recognized a record $22 billion in AI server revenue.

We exited the quarter with a record $132.3 billion of AI server backlog. Behind every customer engagement and every order is a rigorous due diligence process, resulting in a fully vetted backlog. Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power. As I mentioned, each design is bespoke, optimized through multiple iterations with the customer. Through this tight collaboration, we know our customers well and have a high conviction that our backlog will convert to revenue. Our pipeline grew sequentially and remains multiples of our backlog, again, after converting $180 billion over the past 4 quarters. Additionally, our customer base and opportunity pipeline continues to diversify.

We now have over 7,500 Dell AI Factory customers. Our customer base spans neoclouds, sovereigns and enterprises. Within the neocloud segment, we remain highly selective about the partners we work with and the end customers supporting their demand. The global opportunity is expanding as more data centers are built outside of the United States. Across nearly every top country around the world, there are 2 to 3 sovereign projects. Enterprises were the fastest-growing portion of our opportunity pipeline expansion sequentially, providing further evidence that enterprise AI adoption is gaining traction. Internally, we continue to invest in our capabilities, ensuring we maintain our competitive advantage, deliver value for our customers and position for the substantial opportunity ahead. Moving to traditional servers.

Revenue was up 235% as demand remained exceptionally strong, supported by multiple growth drivers that are expanding our TAM. Enterprises increasingly recognize that compute is critical to both the growth and the operations of their business. They are buying more compute to accommodate growing workloads, refreshing their installed base and modernizing their data centers to free up power and space to be positioned for the AI era. Sequentially, we are seeing increased demand for CPU-based compute to support AI and inference workloads. Higher content continues to be a long-term secular tailwind. Servers contain more compute value with higher core counts, greater memory and storage capacity, increasing the value of each system.

Underneath all of this, cyber resilience and security are also driving refresh activity. Much of the installed base requires new hardware to meet current security and performance requirements. These needs cannot always be addressed through a software patch. We are executing very well in a supply-constrained environment, and we expect to gain share this quarter. Turning to storage. Revenue was up 24% as strong demand for our Dell IP portfolio drove revenue growth and improved profitability. Storage has always been critical as enterprise workloads and data grow. In the AI era, it is becoming even more important as data grows at exponential rates. Our storage opportunities are also expanding as AI evolves.

AI workloads are creating new demand drivers like key value caching, context layers and agents that need to store data, memory and state. For an enterprise, its data is its intellectual property, but siloed and without context, it's just data. Agents need that context, and that's why we've expanded the Dell AI Data Platform with a unified semantic layer and an enterprise knowledge graph. Together, they give nearly every application and agent the same trusted current view of the business without rebuilding context from scratch every query. This lowers token consumption, cuts compute costs and speeds time to production, all while keeping the customers' most sensitive data governed inside their own data center. Our storage offerings continue to expand.

Our Dell IP portfolio is resonating with customers, and we expect to gain share this quarter. Demand for Dell IP storage grew for the seventh consecutive quarter, and our Dell IP mix is at an all-time high. Demand remained broad-based with exceptional strength in North America. We also continue to see strong demand for unstructured storage, supporting AI workloads with triple-digit demand growth for the third consecutive quarter. PowerStore delivered a record demand and has now grown double digit or better for 10 consecutive quarters. PowerFlex grew double digits for 3 consecutive quarters and data protection delivered double-digit growth.

Storage growth, greater scale, the mix shift to Dell IP and meaningful sequential improvements in profitability at the solution level continue to be significant drivers for ISG profitability. Our Dell IP performance and accelerating pace of product development give us confidence in the opportunity ahead. Turning to CSG. Revenue grew 3% in a softer PC unit market as the industry adjusts to higher price points. Customers are prioritizing their budgets near term to servers and storage, electing to defer some PC-related refresh. The installed base continues to age, building deferred demand that we expect to refresh in the future. In closing, we continue to deliver a record year with record revenue, EPS, cash generation and capital return to shareholders.

The demand environment we see today remains strong and has not changed. Sophisticated customers are planning years in advance, giving us better visibility into future demand. AI server demand continues to accelerate, supported by a broadening customer base and expanding global opportunity. Our record $132.3 billion of AI server backlog has been fully vetted through our rigorous due diligence process. Traditional server demand remains strong, benefiting from traditional workload growth and aging installed base, heightened security requirements and the growing AI inference demand. Dell IP storage continues to grow and drive incremental profitability. As AI infrastructure becomes more complex, our competitive advantages are more pronounced and our TAM expands, increasing the need for modern disaggregated architecture.

Infrastructure demand continues to outpace supply. As we look into next year, the gap between component supply and end-user demand continues to widen. Our world-class supply chain is well positioned to navigate these constraints and deliver for our customers. Our operating model, speed to market growth and ability to drive scale are producing compounding benefits across the business. Together, these drive significant cash flow, shareholder return and long-term value for our shareholders. I'm proud of the team's performance and expect the momentum to carry into next year. With that, let me turn it over to David to walk through the financials and our outlook.

David Kennedy: Thanks, Jeff. The team executed exceptionally well, driving record revenue, record EPS and record shareholder returns. These results demonstrate the strength of our operating model, which is driving growth, expanding profitability and generating significant cash flow. Total revenue was up 103% to $54.9 billion. Gross margin dollars grew 105% to $11.7 billion. Gross margin rate was 21.2%, up 10 basis points. Operating expenses were up 20% to $3.8 billion, primarily due to variable compensation tied to our outperformance. We continue to drive significant operating leverage with OpEx down 480 basis points to 7% of revenue. Operating income grew 213% to $7.8 billion.

That OpEx obviously allows us then to absorb as we -- you see AI server grow almost 3x year-on-year. We're able to absorb that into the rate.

You saw ISG op inc up almost 5 points year-on-year to 17% of revenue. And ultimately, as we look into Q4, you're seeing more of the same. We've added revenue dollars. We've added margin dollars. We've added rate. So we've taken up the guide across the board in relation to that. And ultimately, that's what we'll look to do, continue to drive and see revenue growth totally decoupled from that, the OpEx performance. Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Sure, Amit. I mean, look, as we have moved through the year, I think we've been consistently saying this demand is durable. The appetite or the demand for intelligence broadly continues. We've seen no slowdown of that. I think our AI orders of another $60 billion quarter. We now have $180 billion of orders in the last 4 quarters. We've shipped nearly $66 billion. All the while, the 5-quarter pipeline continues to build. We've added 4,500 Dell AI factory customers in the last 3 quarters. It was 3,000 in the first 8 quarters. It continues to grow. There are more customers in our 5-quarter pipeline than we have served to date.

All signs are pointing to the continued demand appetite for intelligence, particularly as we've moved from a training, which has driven the market initially to now inference making our way and progressing to agentic and ultimately to recursive learning. We see the pattern continuing. And in fact, we would say for the first 3 years of -- November '22 through October of '25, it was essentially a market driven by single shot sort of AI, you ask it a question, you get an answer. Now we're seeing that change where AI is becoming the doer or the operator. And we're seeing that same benefit inside of our own company.

David spoke to our record low operating expenditures and our modernization activities, all driven by the fact that we are seeing tremendous efficiency in our organization driven by now agentic. And we fundamentally look at this, you get asked why that's the case. It's real simple. Work is really 3 components. There's a component of work that you define what it is, you actually do it and you verify it. The action, the operating of the work is being increasingly moved towards agentic. And that is driving, we believe, an incredible growth rate in tokens and token consumption, the infrastructure that goes along with it, and we don't see that slowing down.

So when I look at the growth categories in our business and whether that's in our storage business, whether that's in our traditional server business and certainly on the AI side, it's inference, it's agentic. We're seeing KV cache need. We're seeing recursive learning need. We're seeing the agentic inference need, the resulting harnesses to operate this. And our forecast remain, I think, unchanged from the last time we talked about this topic. We still see tremendous token growth through the end of the decade. 87x, I think, was the last number I talked about, 3,600 quadrillion tokens. Training demand continues to grow 5x.

We're still tracking over 200 gigawatts of build-out of shells and power to provide the homes for all of this compute capability that is being needed. So again, no slowdown. I look at our own use inside our company. Our token growth is greater today than it was when the fiscal year began. Our use of agents, any given day, there are 100,000 agents spun up across our organization by our developers and knowledge workers consuming tokens. David Kennedy: Yes. I guess to build on it in relation to the credit and capital element of that discussion. Again, like Jeff said, it's not a new process. Operator: And we'll go next to Katherine Murphy with Goldman Sachs.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Sure. Let me start with the server units question that you asked. Look, very directly, server units were down. We expected that. There has been significant unit TAM destruction with the inflation that has been in the marketplace. If you take what has traditionally been 20% of the units, which have been 1P towers and 1P racks, that would have been 20-ish percent of the units, 2% of the revenue. That market under $3,000 servers is gone. So industry-wise, there are fewer units.

But what's interesting and I think very telling is the content of every server that we sold and shipped in the quarter was significantly different. Let me explain a little bit. So as we think about value and you think about these ratios that I mentioned earlier where an 18G server can consolidate 12 to 14 of our old 14G servers, that's built on a premise they're more capable. That capability is built on more cores, more DRAM and more NAND. We shipped and sold more cores in Q3 than we did the previous quarter and year-over-year.

We shipped more cores and more -- or excuse me, more bits of DRAM per server than we did last quarter and last year. And we shipped more bytes of storage in the servers we shipped this quarter than we did last quarter and last year. So the content per server is going up significantly, not inflation adjusted, absolute content, more cores, more bits, more DRAM per server, more productive, more powerful servers capable of being deployed, albeit in fewer units, taking on significantly greater workloads. That's what we're seeing in the marketplace. That has been, I think, consistent trend now for several quarters, and I think that will continue going forward.

On the storage side, a very -- it's a different trend, but a similar outcome. What we're seeing is greater attach of our higher-value storage products, our Dell IP portfolio. The Dell IP portfolio, we ran across a bunch of numbers, but 7 consecutive quarters of growth now. I think PowerStore has grown 10 consecutive quarters of double-digit growth. The unstructured products continue to grow quite nicely. The demand of them was in triple-digit range.

We are seeing more attach of storage in our AI business, particularly around the unstructured products, our PowerScale and ObjectScale product that continues to bode well as we go in the future because the demand drivers for storage in the future around the very same things that I described in servers, the agentic workload, agentic AI, KV cache, multimodal workflows and recursive learning all drive incremental storage. And in fact, incredible amounts of storage as you have to start looking at the traces and logs of every agent. If you start looking at the artifacts the agents create. If you look at some of the retrievable corpora that the agents create.

That is all driving significant storage growth and storage opportunities in the future. Again, it can go on with KV cache, the multimodal workflows when you start going into imaging, you start going to video, audio, sensor drives more bytes of storage that has to be ultimately stored. And ultimately, you're going to see that storage grows and grows and grows not by GPUs that are deployed, but by the bytes that have to be retained and that compound storage over time. Those are the growth drivers. That's where we're seeing the opportunities and where the focus of our business is.

Operator: And we'll move to our next question from David Vogt with UBS.

But would love to kind of get your perspective in terms of where you think pricing goes, demand? Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Well, I'll start with not as inflationary is still a cost increase to our customers in the form of price. And given the significant inflation that's occurred over the past year, even a moderating inflationary number still leads to higher-priced products for our customers. From a macro view, when we look at the supply picture and our supply outlook, there's nothing that suggests that we're going to see price declines in enterprise NAND and DRAM for servers. The demand for those categories of memory continues to be way ahead of the supply. As more DRAM wafer capacity is set forth for GPUs and specifically building HBM, it comes at the expense of all other types of memory.

We think that crunch continues clearly into '27. And while the rate of inflation won't be the same as we saw in '26, we still believe the market is inflationary. Customers are spending their budgets today. We don't -- I don't know of a customer that's on the sideline that doesn't buy as much as they used to, but I'd also tell you that server they're buying today, if it's a 17G or an 18G server from us, is significantly more capable than the thing that it's replacing. So if you were to take a 14G that we sold 5 years ago, 4 years ago, and it's being retired, that product was $7,500, give or take.

And while they're tying all of the questions together, while that may mean fewer units, it's a more capable machine, and that is what's being deployed in small businesses to the largest corporations in the world to meet their needs. But customers aren't on the sideline in servers. It would be different if we were talking about PCs. I think companies are deferring their PC purchases to ensure they have the infrastructure to work in what is going to be a very disruptive era with agentic technology really reinventing companies.

And that's what we see happening in the marketplace. So do I think the rate of increase slows? Yes. Do I still think that a significant price implication to our customers? Yes, because a smaller percentage on a large number is still a lot of dollars. Customers are spending their budgets. We see them active in the marketplace, and we believe that will continue into '27.

David Kennedy: And I think, Jeff, to build on that, I think the customers are trying to be resourceful and agile there, too, in terms of our DFS offering. So for investment-grade customers, the originations growth we've seen in PCs, storage and servers, up 55% in Q3. So you can see there's an appetite and the need to get infrastructure built out. So even in a budget crunch in the near term, the ability to turn CapEx into OpEx and understand what that looks like is a differentiated capability that we have in the marketplace. And I think our customers have appreciated the flexibility and being able to take advantage of that as part of their IT build-out.

Timothy (Tim) Long: I wanted to go back to the traditional server, some of the comments you made about a little bit more CPU type of servers to neoclouds and probably to sovereigns as well. Curious if you could just somehow quantify the pace or how that's looking, how margins look for those type of products? And then when you're selling these customers CPU servers compared to GPU servers, is the attach rate different? So maybe if you could just scale kind of how big and strong that business is and what it means for some of the other dynamics that we look at across the business?

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Sure. Let me try. A traditional server sold into a non-GPU application, and we separate the business, there's a GPU, that's the AI server business. It's not the largest portion of our traditional server business, which is our traditional enterprises and traditional applications, the things that we've talked about before. When I think about these servers going into these new workloads, it is across neoclouds who are deploying them that's in the financial services market.

It's in the EDA market, it's in the semis market, high-frequency traders, pharma, et cetera, they're very advanced in their AI deployments. They are driving agentic AI across their enterprises. And we believe that market continues to grow as the next iteration or evolution of agentic takes place, which is recursive learning. All of that drives more compute. More agents, more compute. The harness is essential to this. And the harness and the work that the harness does is really a CPU task. It's these things about how you manage containers, how do you manage sandboxes, manage I/O, how do you orchestrate that workload, which is CPU-driven is what we're talking about here.

And I referenced earlier, those types of servers are roughly twice the ASP as an enterprise-class server running an enterprise workload. The margins in those classes of devices as all of our -- across our server portfolio is well within our product-by-product internal marks that we make for our server products, and we feel very comfortable about that business and the prospects of growth are significant.

Paul Frantz: All right. And Jeff, please close it out.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Sure. Thanks, Paul, and thanks, everyone, for joining us today. Demand continues to exceed supply, and our world-class supply chain positions us well to capitalize on the opportunity. We are looking forward to Q4 and capping off a record year. Our full year revenue guidance of $202 billion and non-GAAP diluted EPS of $29.68, nearly up 190%. We head into FY '28 with strong momentum and confidence in our ability to continue creating long-term value for shareholders. Thanks again for your time today. Happy Thanksgiving to everyone.

Subscription revenue rose 12.8% as AI products gained traction.

Workday (WDAY +1.79%) reported third-quarter results highlighted by an acceleration in AI-driven bookings and an upward revision to its full-year profitability and revenue guidance. Management reported that the company is evolving its business model through the expansion of flex credits and the general availability of its agentic platform, which allows customers to deploy autonomous agents for HR, finance, and IT workflows. The company recently completed its acquisition of C1.ai to integrate identity governance for both human and AI workers, positioning itself as a central security layer for the hybrid enterprise. Management stated that the innovation cycle has reached its highest velocity since the company's inception, with new products like Workday Data Cloud and Sana meeting robust customer interest across global markets.

Tal Liani: Hi, guys. I have a very high level question. When I see your results and I look at Salesforce and ServiceNow, I see companies that really try hard on AI. But the core business is either flat or down. And the question I have is. At the high level is, I understand that you have great technology. I see. I can see the product. But look at it from the customer point of view. What drives the customer to deploy your solution? Is it where is the money gonna come from?

Meaning, if they need to spend more on AI, will it be at the expense of the other licenses that they spend with you, or will it be new budgets? And if it is new budgets, then what is the reason? Meaning, what do they get from it that justifies it? Thanks.

Aneel Bhusri: Maybe I will start it with that. No. it is it is a it is a great question. You know, I would say there are some markets in the US in particular, like the Fortune 500 market. We are fairly well penetrated and those customers. And that is been the case before AI. That our opportunity is to go back into that base and sell them more. And I feel very grateful that AI showed up because we have a wave of new products that add tremendous value to our customers that they are adopting. When we go into next year, we do need to refocus back on the core applications.

I think the whole world's gotten really excited and carried away with AI. But the core applications are still doing quite well. Salespeople like to sell the new stuff, and this new stuff is selling well. As it relates to the budget, I think, to be honest, it is a bit of both. there is an AI budget that is separate from HR and finance. And then there is a budget for HR and finance. And trying to figure out ways. Do they buy a new module from Workday, or do they buy flex credits and new AI products? And so I think that is really the conversation that is happening.

And as I talked about the go to market changes going into next year, we have gotta be very focused on both core business as well as the new AI products and incent the salespeople accordingly.

Gerrit (Garrett) Kazmaier: And I think, you know, there is, you know, I think, you know, the framing for our customers is, you know, really value driven. For instance, they look into the spend in shared service centers. They look in how much they are spending on HR case delivery. Which are substantial amounts of money for them. For them, the ability to convert, you know, a very high spend into a smaller software spend with us it is really compelling. So it is not like a software-to-software transition. They are looking at their company spend all up in any specific function. And, frankly, they are seeing AI leverage with that. Right?

And that is where they can free up money or can divert, you know, funds for growing or stay flat with headcount like we do, and reinvest that into AI automation. that is where we are seeing lift across all of our products. You know, from Xtend to Sana Learn to Data Cloud to our agents. They are basically tapping into that opportunity, and our customers are not seeing it as a constraint or contradiction if they are running software spend.

Operator: We will now take 2 more questions. Next question comes from the line of Rishi Jaluria with RBC Capital Markets. Rishi, please go ahead.

Rishi Jaluria: Oh, wonderful. Thanks so much for taking my questions. Maybe just a simple 1 on, you know, thinking through the impact of AI on margins, not even right now, but over the next, you know, 1 or 2 years, you are you are seeing nice early adoption of AI throughout your customer base. You are talking about further ARR inflection going from here. Maybe 2 pieces to that, though. As we think about just greater usage and credit adoption, what sort of tools do you have, whether it is multimodality, efficiency or something else to kind of protect your own gross margins from AI, putting aside the public cloud that you just talked about. And same with the FDEs. Right?

I recognize you are working with Accenture, but as we think about just getting. Doing more handholding, having, you know, more human resource intensiveness, what. How should we think about the impact of that on your overall margins? And, again, any tools you have to kind of protect yourself from margin degradation as you see that inflection in AI adoption in the customer base. Thanks.

Aneel Bhusri: Yeah. You know, I personally see it as margin expansion. I love the consumption model. it is a model that I have always admired the hyperscalers have that more scale and more usage drive more margin. You know, the FTEs, the beauty of that model is that you get these agents live in weeks, not years. And as soon as the agents are live, they are they are producing revenue and consumption for work day. And to the question you asked about the multimodal, we are absolutely multimodal. We are always choosing the lowest cost path from a foundational model perspective. I will let Garrett talk more about that.

But when we look at the future of consumption and what we can do with agents and be very efficient with it, I think it is actually a margin expanding opportunity.

Gerrit (Garrett) Kazmaier: Yeah. Like Anil has said, right, you know, this is a largely unoptimized space, you know, in AI overall. We are, you know, deliberately being multimodal and having active model routing because of many of the tasks that we are doing You know, the previous generation's models are already saturating our evaluation and accuracy criteria. We have an enormous range of models that we can deploy and really, you know, strike the right price performance characteristics that we need. So we do not feel that we have any cost or margin pressure from different tier models. You know, quite the opposite, actually.

We just announced our partnership with Safe AI and Jasper, which are adding a new component on model routing to it, making it efficient. We have just increased the coverage of our models that we are using internally or across our AI agents. And as Anil has said, you know, actually, frankly, we feel there is an opportunity for us to expand rather than see compression on the margin side because the space overall is unoptimized. And the way how we have approached it by being model agnostic, being task specific, and partnering with all of the model providers on picking the right models for any specific task has so far really paid dividends for us.

Rishi Jaluria: Alright. Very helpful. Thank you.

Operator: Your last question comes from the line of Scott Berg with Needham. Scott, please go ahead.

Scott Berg: Hi. Thanks for taking questions here. I wanted to follow-up on the FDE commentary. I know there is been a couple of questions asked, but you have gotten into this with Accenture, and I assume the other partnerships will be of similar going forward, How do you think about the long term opportunities with those customers? Will this fundamentally change maybe the amount of software agents that you are able to sell these customers? Or is it really more just about speeding up the delivery and the use case of them? A question I get asked often. Does it actually change the size of the pie? Or just does it allow the Thanksgiving pie to be eaten more quickly? Thanks.

Aneel Bhusri: I think it is definitely both. there is no question it speeds up. Speeds up usage. You know, when we think about a typical cloud software deployment, a year used to be a great standard. Maybe now you can get it in 6 months for a large enterprise. We are talking about weeks for agents. And, you know, a lot of the agents are built on the same dataset. And so once the partner or Workday is in there, solving 1 problem with the data and with the agent, they can move on to other problems. And it is all it is all gonna be about discovery on the customer side, figuring out what problems they are looking to solve.

And so now have 17 agents in the market. That list will continue to grow. And I would hope that you would see these customers adopting many agents. Think the self-service and Workday concierge are good places to start, but the work intelligence 1 it is kind of a no brainer. You can see how 4 or 5 agents could be up and running pretty quickly, and so it is not 1 and done and that. And that is a pattern we are seeing even in the early days of adoption.

Scott Berg: Very helpful. Thanks for taking my questions.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, this concludes the Q&A. Thank you for your participation in today's conference. You may now disconnect.

#2976. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

#2975. College Scholarship Breakdown: Types, Sponsors and Eligibility at a Glance

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Scholarships vary in what they pay for and who can apply. Understanding the differences can save you time during your application process.

Scholarships have become a standard part of applying for college. You can learn about scholarships in a variety of ways, but looking through an online database of available scholarships — the most common way — can be overwhelming.

Before you go searching for a scholarship, it's important to understand the types of scholarships available and how to identify the ones that give you the best chance of winning, which can save you time and potentially earn you more funding. Here’s what you need to know about scholarships to decide which ones are best for you.

Scholarships are often funded by three groups: private organizations, institutions like universities, and government agencies. None is better than the other when it comes to awarding funds.

Nonprofit organizations and clubs that are looking for students either majoring in or researching certain fields, or who have experience volunteering in a specific field.

Companies that want to support all students or only fund those majoring in a field that relates to the companies’ industries.

Financial institutions, such as banks or credit unions, that want to support their community or their members.

Individuals or families that are funding private scholarships, usually in memory of a loved one.

Universities and colleges that are offering funds to students who attend their campuses.

Research organizations that want to fund students who will research in their areas of interest and further their causes.

These scholarships generally are provided by local, state or federal government agencies for a variety of reasons. Despite being funded by a government agency, the scholarships do not require you to pay back the money — unlike federal student loans.

Some scholarships pay for anything related to college expenses, including tuition, room and board, books and supplies, and more. Other scholarships limit what you can pay for with the funds, such as only tuition or tuition along with books. It’s important to look at this restriction when applying for scholarships to ensure the funds will go toward what you need to cover.

Merit scholarships require you to show excellence or achievements in your schoolwork, through talents and abilities, and even leadership or service work. Because these types of awards can be highly competitive, merit scholarships might require more than just achievements, such as volunteer or leadership experience. This means merit-based scholarships can overlap with other types of scholarship categories. Here are some examples of merit-based scholarships:

Merit scholarships often require you to have earned a minimum grade point average (GPA). The minimum GPA depends on the scholarship but often ranges from 2.0 to 4.0, with more competitive scholarships usually requiring higher GPAs. Scholarships with lower GPA minimums are more likely to consider additional factors, such as financial need.

Some merit scholarships might require a minimum ACT or SAT score instead of a GPA — or in addition to a minimum GPA.

Merit scholarships might also require applicants to have participated in activities outside of their schoolwork. This is common for scholarships that require membership in a certain group or organization. For example, membership in agricultural clubs, such as 4-H or FFA, and scouting groups, such as the National Eagle Scout Association, appear in scholarship requirements.

Some scholarships emphasize volunteering or community service and only consider applicants who have that experience. Applications vary in how detailed their requirements can be. Some scholarships want only a general description of where and how you’ve volunteered, and others might require experience with a service project that shows more leadership experience or time volunteering with a certain type of organization.

Scholarships that are awarded to students who can’t afford college are called need-based scholarships.

Unmet financial need is the difference between what it will cost you to attend college and what you can afford to pay. Because calculating how much you can afford is a complicated process, many scholarships refer to your FAFSA to document your financial need.

Some scholarship requirements may be as straightforward as demonstrating that you have financial need, but some scholarships might have income limits. However, income restrictions are less common.

Athletic scholarships are for — you guessed it — athletes. They are usually offered by colleges and universities to recruit athletes onto their collegiate teams and can be competitive. Which sports have scholarships available and the scholarship amounts vary by college.

Even though the main criterion for an athletic scholarship is being good at your sport, you’ll likely still need to show that you can keep up with your schoolwork. Most athletic scholarships require students to earn a minimum GPA or test scores to remain eligible while they’re in college.

Some scholarships are designated for students majoring in a general field, such as science or education, but others can be for very specific areas of study. For example, a scholarship for students majoring in a natural resource field could include majors in biology, ecology, wildlife biology, conservation education, forestry, soils and hydrology. However, a stricter scholarship might state that students have to major in more specific topics, such as biochemistry or microbial ecology.

Scholarships are available for active and former members of the military and members of their families. In addition to federal funds available for veterans to attend college, private organizations and some universities have scholarships for veterans to offset the cost of a degree.

Which family members can apply for funds depends on the individual scholarship. For example, some scholarships extend to children or spouses of veterans, but some go as far in a family tree as great-grandchildren.

Veteran- and military-focused scholarships might require that applicants or their family members enlisted in a certain branch, served during a particular time or conflict, or meet a certain rank or status such as receiving disability. Scholarships might also require that the applicant be a wartime veteran or family member of a wartime veteran; not all veterans meet this status.

Scholarships are also awarded to people who identify with a certain group. Common examples of identity-based scholarships include those for people who have disabilities, belong to certain ethnic or religious groups, identify as LGBTQIA+ or are first-generation students. Some identity-based scholarships require applicants to meet several criteria, such as belonging to more than one identity group.

Outside of what would be considered standard DEI groups, there are scholarships for applicants who identify with less common groups, such as veganism, homelessness and model railroad builders.

The best scholarships for you depend on your situation. For example, if you are a skilled athlete with a good academic record, going for an athletic scholarship might give you the most funding. On the other hand, if you’re going to research a topic that isn’t common, looking for scholarships that support your research topic might be your best bet because competition could be lower.

Good tactics to figure out which scholarships are worth your time include:

Think of the skills, talents, experience and identities that are unique to you. For example, being a child of a veteran immediately qualifies you for scholarships with fewer applicants than scholarships open to everyone. Likewise, if you embrace a certain ethnicity, identify with a specific group or have experience with a type of work, you might qualify for scholarships that appreciate and recognize those attributes more than the average scholarship.

Apply if you think you're eligible. Don’t apply to just a few scholarships and hope you get them. Instead, apply for as many scholarships as you can and for which you’re eligible. This increases your chances of receiving funds. Even small scholarships can make a big impact when you add several of them together.

Understand how you can use the money. If you already have a scholarship that covers only books, applying for the same type of scholarship isn’t helpful if you don’t need the extra funds. Instead, look for scholarships that cover the costs you have remaining.

Not sure where to look? Our sister site Scholarships360.org provides students with vetted scholarship opportunities. That would be a good place to start.
