Grants don’t have to be repaid, but the money can only go toward school-related costs. Here’s how to use grants to pay for school and how to make them go further.

Grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education. It’s free money you aren’t expected to pay back.

Grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses. Some grants, depending on who awards them, require an application or have requirements you must meet before you can get your money.

Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.

Federal grants come from the federal government.

State grants come from state programs and often can only be used at schools in that state.

Institutional grants come from your college or university, or even your program or major.

Private grants come from nonprofits, community organizations and individual donors.

To receive a federal grant, you must complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). Most states require the FAFSA for state grants, and a few require a separate state application. You’ll need to complete the FAFSA for each year you’re enrolled in school. You may need to meet certain eligibility requirements, such as income limits, to get some grants. The FAFSA is how you apply for the Pell Grant, which is a financial need-based grant. The FAFSA also determines eligibility for federal work-study, which is a job program rather than a grant.

Federal aid, including federal grants, typically requires students to meet satisfactory academic progress. This means you have to maintain a minimum grade point average and be on track to finish your degree on time, as determined by your school. Your school also sets how many credits you must take to qualify for grant funding.

Some grants — typically private or institutional grants — require an additional application that asks for transcripts, letters of recommendation and personal essays. Your school’s financial aid office or the grant provider will have details on applying for specific grants.

After you submit the FAFSA, you’ll receive a financial aid award letter from each school you applied to, which outlines how much in federal, state and institutional grants you’ve been offered. You must accept your aid to receive it.

Most grants will be disbursed directly to your college or university. Your school will apply the grant money first to tuition, fees and any other charges it bills, such as housing or a meal plan.

In some cases, you may receive more grant money than your school bills, which is the best-case scenario. If that happens to you, any leftover funds will likely be refunded to you. Refund timelines vary by school, so it may take some time to get your money. You can get your refund faster by setting up direct deposit with your school. You can then use the funds for other costs approved by your grant — some examples are detailed below.

If you have questions about your grant money, contact your college’s financial aid office.

Grants can help cover cost-of-attendance expenses. Generally, you can use grant money to pay for tuition, textbooks, class materials, transportation, housing and food. Depending on your school’s policies, you can use grant money to cover summer classes or study abroad programs, too.

Some grants come with specific terms about how you can spend them. Check your financial aid award letter or, for a private or institutional grant, the school’s or organization’s website to find specifics.

After your grant is applied to your tuition and school expenses, you can options to fill the gaps between what the grant covers and the total cost of your program. Some options include savings, scholarships, work-study, payment plans, federal student loans or, as a last resort, private loans. By using grants to pay for your college education, you may be able to borrow less.

To maximize the grants you’re eligible to receive, enter accurate information on the FAFSA and complete it as soon as you can — some funds are first-come, first-served. Also, don’t limit yourself to federal or state grants — search and apply for as many privately funded grants as you can find.

Your grant money usually goes straight to your college or university to pay your tuition and fees. Anything that is left over may be disbursed to you for other school-related costs.

Yes, but it depends on your grant. Housing is part of your cost of attendance, so you can use grant money to pay for off-campus rent.

You don’t have to pay back a grant as long as you continue to meet all requirements for the grant, such as staying enrolled. You can use grant money on school and school-related expenses. Some grants may require you to meet eligibility requirements such as a minimum GPA or state residency. If you receive more grant money than your cost of attendance for a given school term, ask your financial aid office if you can put that grant money toward next year’s cost of attendance.

If you have a federal grant like a Pell Grant, these are examples when you may have to repay all or part of the grant:

You received enough scholarship money to reduce your federal aid need.

It depends. You can usually use grant money to buy a laptop. Computers are considered course materials, which fall under cost-of-attendance expenses, so they can be covered by a grant. However, always double-check with the grant provider and your financial aid award letter to ensure that you’re following all restrictions. Whether you can use grant money to cover a laptop depends on your school’s policies and how much grant money you receive.

If you get more grant money than your school bills you, you’ll likely receive the leftover money to spend on other cost-of-attendance expenses. You can use this money on living costs such as transportation or housing. Grant money often goes mostly toward tuition, so a refund isn’t guaranteed.

Grant and scholarship money is generally tax-free when you use it for tuition, required fees, books and required class supplies. If you have additional questions, consider talking to a tax professional.

#2947. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

#2946. Costco Hasn't Split Its Stock Since 2000. Here's Why 2027 Could Be the Year.

A four-digit share price has investors wondering if a stock split is on the table next year.

By Neil Patel – Nov 25, 2026 at 12:00AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Costco Wholesale ›

Forward stock splits receive a lot of attention from investors. It might be because this move reminds shareholders how well the business has performed in the past. And it's a signal of confidence from the management team that executives are optimistic about the future. Investor psychology gets a boost.

If we focus just on the fundamentals, nothing really changes. Operations resume as normal. The same employees sell the same products and services to the same customers. It's business as usual.

The data is still worth highlighting. According to Bank of America and Bloomberg, companies that undergo a forward stock split see their share prices rise an average of 25% over the subsequent 12 months. Naturally, investors try to figure out who the next big candidates are, so they can potentially capture sizable gains in their portfolios.

This brings up Costco (COST +2.23%). It hasn't split its stock since 2000, but it could take action next year. Here's why.

Costco's board of directors approved a 2-for-1 split on Dec. 2, 1999. It took effect on Jan. 14, 2000, turning a roughly $98 stock into a $49 one.

The business was performing well. Net revenue jumped 16% year over year in Q1 2020, and net income totaled $129.3 million.

Shares were pricey, too. The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio hit 44.3 at the start of 2000. In that era, split-adjusted prices were the standard way to keep an expensive stock within reach of everyday investors.

Fast-forward to today. Costco closed at $1,097.91 on Nov. 23, more than 11 times the price that triggered the last split. In fiscal 2026 (ended Aug. 30), net sales rose 10.1% to $297.2 billion, and diluted earnings per share (EPS) climbed 14% to $20.76. The trailing P/E is near 53.

Record share price. Healthy growth. A premium valuation. Today's setup rhymes with 2000.

Rival Walmart also split 3-for-1 in February 2024. This was partly to help employees buy shares.

But management hasn't tipped its hand. On the fiscal 2025 first-quarter call in December 2024, chief financial officer Gary Millerchip said, "There isn't a plan at this time for a stock split." He pointed to fractional-share trading, but said Costco would keep evaluating the idea.

Executives are clearly confident in the company's position. On Nov. 10, the board declared a $30 per-share special dividend worth $13.3 billion. With the share price above $1,000, however, the split question probably won't go away in 2027.

Front-running a stock split is a short-term game. Long-term investors can avoid it. Bank of America's research still found that about 30% of split stocks fell over the following 12 months.

There's a much simpler approach to follow: Find businesses worth owning for five years or more. Costco makes the grade.

Its massive scale lets it buy in bulk, keep markups low, and still run lean. Overhead costs ate up just 8.9% of Q4 merchandise sales.

Members are fiercely loyal. The U.S. and Canada renewal rate hit 92.3%. And paid memberships grew 3.8% to 84.1 million households in the fourth quarter. Demand is steady, with worldwide traffic up 3.3%.

And profits keep rising. Net income grew 46% from $6.3 billion in fiscal 2023 to $9.2 billion in fiscal 2026.

This company belongs on every long-term investor's watch list. But the price tag causes hesitation.

Costco's P/E ratio is 159% more expensive than the S&P 500. The market seemingly always places a premium on this retail stock. A wonderful business can still be a disappointing investment at the wrong price, however.

With Costco, quality is never in doubt. The real question is always valuation.

#2931. 19 Signs Your Company’s Technology Is Creating More Work

Technology should simplify workflows and improve productivity. However, when systems are difficult to navigate, unreliable or disconnected, employees may develop alternative solutions just to get their jobs done.

These workarounds can reveal deeper problems with technology adoption, system design and organizational processes. Below, Forbes Technology Council members share warning signs that employees are spending too much time working around their company’s technology rather than benefiting from it, along with insights on addressing the underlying issues.

The biggest tell for me is hearing, “Here’s how we actually do it.” If that follows with some description that combines spreadsheets, duplicate data entry, manual handoffs or clever ways around the system, that’s a pretty clear sign the technology is creating work rather than removing it. - Abhijit Singh, Jefferson

If employees constantly ask coworkers for help with the same system tasks or there’s an unofficial cheat sheet, chat thread or go-to “expert” everyone relies on to navigate a tool, the technology is not intuitive enough to be used on its own. Low adoption of mandatory tools or new hires taking too long to be productive with a tool are indicators that people are spending too much time figuring out the technology instead of using it. - Austin Berglas, Nardello & Co.

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Working around a system can increase your cognitive load—the mental effort placed on your working memory. A recent survey found that since AI was introduced, enterprise workers spend longer searching for information, parse through more alerts, and juggle more tabs and applications. Symptoms like these can indicate employees are working harder to manage the technology than realizing its benefits. - Mazy Dar, HERE Enterprise (here.io)

Jumping across multiple tools and screens to complete one workflow is a clear sign that people are just becoming workers for the tools rather than using those tools to deliver their work better and faster. This is more relevant in the AI era. - Raja Shanmugam, TATA Consultancy Services

When employees rely on personal texts, phone calls or spreadsheets to compensate for enterprise systems, there’s a workflow problem. These workarounds often emerge because existing tools are too slow, fragmented or unreliable. Leaders should investigate where employees bypass technology and address the underlying friction before it creates operational risks. - Judit Sharon, OnPage Corporation

Watch for employees delaying decisions because they don’t trust how current the information is. If a sales or marketing team has to wait for an overnight update before responding to a customer or adjusting a campaign, the technology is setting the pace instead of supporting the work. Teams should be able to act on what is happening now, not yesterday’s picture. - Vibhor Kapoor, AdRoll

One sign is that unofficial spreadsheets become essential to completing everyday work. In capital markets, employees may repeatedly export trade data, reconcile it manually, and re-enter the results across systems. When these workarounds become routine, the technology is shifting effort onto employees rather than removing it. Those spreadsheets reveal where workflows need fixing. - Lakshmanan Alagappan, Genpact UK

Shadow documentation is a sign that the official documentation is lacking or so generic that it is hard to adapt to use cases that are fairly common. The more guides that are built to explain how to use a piece of software, the more it should be evaluated for improvement. Simplify the interface with role-based views, and rename custom fields and data so they’re clearer. Just don’t forget to clean up the shadow documentation too. - Luke Wallace, Bottle Rocket

One sign is that the know-how lives in people, not the system. When a tool doesn’t do exactly what’s needed, rather than asking for changes to the tool, work becomes manual, and one person ends up as the only one who knows how it really runs. Sometimes that’s accidental and sometimes it’s job security; either way, it’s a bottleneck. - Anila Siraj, OpsBridge Advisory

One sign is employees building integrations the vendor never intended. Not plugins. Not configurations. Custom code written at midnight by someone who needed two systems to talk to each other and could not wait six months for a roadmap update. That unauthorized integration is not ingenuity. It is your architecture silently fracturing one undocumented API call at a time. When engineers route around the system, the system has already failed. - Mukul Arora

People clicking straight through warnings is a sign. Track override rates and fix the friction behind them. If employees routinely hit “proceed anyway” on a blocked link or a security prompt, the tool is getting in the way of real work, and they have stopped reading it. That is a workaround too, albeit a quiet one, and it trains them to ignore warnings—maybe even those that matter. - Flavius Plesu, OutThink

One clear sign is when employees spend more time figuring out how to make a tool work than doing their actual jobs. If everyone knows which buttons to avoid, which errors to ignore and when to restart the system, your technology isn’t saving time. It’s wasting it. - Margarita Simonova, ILoveMyQA

Check the expense reports, not the help desk tickets. When employees start reimbursing themselves for $30 SaaS subscriptions, they’ve already given up on the official tools and bought their way around them. Finance sees it first. IT sees it months later. The line items are small enough to approve without question, which is exactly why they keep adding up. - Nidhi Jain, CloudEagle.ai

Map the value stream from user intent to task outcome. If employees are required to navigate more than three non-value-added steps to complete a task, I’d question the process before adding more steps. Workarounds add effort yet little to no customer value. Even worse is when teams automate workarounds when they should be eliminating the reason it exists in the first place. - April Ho-Nishimura, Infineon Technologies AG

When I ask a client team how their leadership report is produced, a common answer is that someone builds a spreadsheet by hand before every meeting. That tells me the official systems are being worked around. The hours are the visible cost. The bigger one is that leaders start questioning the numbers in the room instead of making decisions. - Dimitar Dimitrov, Accedia

Count the decisions the technology changed last week. Many companies hand managers a data platform and announce that every number is in there, ready for any table they want. Almost nobody opens it because it asks them to become analysts. They keep deciding using their gut and old reports. A tool that shows each manager their own score and the next move gets checked daily. If a system doesn’t trigger decisions, it is overhead. - Vivek Thomas, AISensum

You must watch how often employees double-check a tool’s output before acting on it. If a manager has to pull the original records to verify every report, the system may be saving time on preparation while adding it back in review. So, ask what people still check by hand and why. That extra checking is part of the cost of the tool, too. - Elton Chan, Second Talent

Take a construction site where the real system is WhatsApp. A delivery gets redirected to another site in a group chat; nobody updates the records, materials arrive at the wrong site, and machinery stands idle. When orders change in chats and handwritten logs, the ERP is just a reporting duty. Count how many changes never reach your system of record. - Andrew Babkin, Azati

One sign is when employees lower the quality of their work because company technology cannot support enough detail. Engineers may simplify technical assessments, while customer service teams may give incomplete responses because systems restrict what they can record or process. Leaders should check whether technology limitations influence the quality of business outcomes. Technology should support professional judgment, not force employees to compromise it. - Salice Thomas, Wipro Limited

#2926. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

Frank Cappelleri is the founder and president of CappThesis, an independent research firm that helps active investors through time-tested chart and statistical analysis. Prior to starting CappThesis, he spent 25 years on Wall Street as an equity sales trader, technical analyst, research sales specialist and desk strategist.

As inflation continues to squeeze household budgets, consumers are increasingly becoming selective about where to spend their money. As a result, discount retailers are back in vogue. Shoppers are looking to squeeze every last bit of value from every dollar spent.

Even middle- and higher-income households are looking for better value on daily-use and household essential items. And that's where Dollar Tree (DLTR +11.18%) has taken advantage of the circumstances, attracting more customers with an expanded assortment of merchandise and pricing it competitively.

The discount retailer's latest quarterly results for the 13 weeks ending Oct. 31 strongly suggest that it is more than just an occasional bargain-shopping destination. Dollar Tree is now part of customers' regular shopping routines.

Dollar Tree's multipricing strategy has increased customer traffic. Image source: Getty Images.

Customer traffic rose a solid 3.8% over this period, up from the 0.4% increase in the second quarter. Comparable-store sales also rose a healthy 4.6% while total revenue increased nearly 7%, to about $5.1 billion.

Adjusted earnings per share (EPS), the core profit marker for Wall Street, crushed estimates by more than 25%, coming in at $1.16 versus average estimates of $0.92. Stronger-than-expected sales, improved merchandise costs, better expense management, and lower shrink all contributed to the bottom line.

Essentially, management's turnaround strategy is working. When customers respond with higher footfall, it means there's an improved shopping experience, usually driven by a superior merchandise assortment.

More importantly, the dollar store witnessed growth across customer income groups. In the earnings call, CEO Mike Creedon explained that while lower-income shoppers constitute the largest share of the customer base, middle- and higher-income customers (known as trade-in or trade-down customers in retail parlance) have contributed to over half of the growth. These customers may visit Dollar Tree stores only four to six times a year. Yet their seasonal or holiday shopping cumulatively generates $1 billion in sales for every additional visit, according to Creedon.

Traditionally, Dollar Tree operated on its hugely popular single $ 1.25 price point model. But moving to a multi-tier pricing strategy (or multi-price strategy) over the last few quarters has helped the retailer expand its merchandise assortment, particularly in discretionary and seasonal goods, which has proved popular with higher-income customers.

That said, the loyalists -- the retailer's traditional, price-sensitive core customers who visit its stores more than 70 times a year -- continue to drive the business's foundational revenue.

The bigger investor takeaway is that a multi-price strategy enabled customers to combine traditional single-price-point items with multi-price products in a single transaction. These mixed baskets accounted for 25% of transactions and half of total sales. So, essentially, this strategy does more than increase average transaction values (or "average ticket"). It's encouraging shoppers to purchase a wider array of products during each visit.

Dollar Tree has done its homework to make shopping more convenient and encourage repeat visits. The retailer completed 3,000 store refreshes and renovations across its store base, focusing on "brighter, cleaner, and more inviting stores."

This includes raising store operating standards, improving merchandising and product availability, and simplifying routines for store employees.

Additionally, the company's "It's All in the Tree" nationwide marketing campaign, which communicates its expanded assortment while reinforcing the value and convenience available at its stores, has played a major role in increasing traffic.

Not surprisingly, Dollar Tree's stronger showing in the third quarter prompted management to raise its fiscal 2026 earnings forecast to $8.05 to $8.25 per share from a previous range of $7.70 to $8.05, a significant 35% increase at the midpoint. The company also reported solid cash generation, with free cash flow reaching $122 million on an operating cash flow totaling $375 million.

However, investors might overlook that overall profitability declined this quarter, with gross margin declining 10 basis points to 35.7%, while adjusted operating margin fell 120 basis points to 6.1%. Management acknowledged that continued inflationary pressures, higher fuel and freight costs, and product cost inflation have weighed on profitability.

Importantly, management expects the fuel- and freight-driven inflationary environment to persist into 2027. But will the company be equipped to handle these pressures? I think so. The third quarter was a demonstration of just that.

However, growth rates could still slow down. Mixed baskets generated nearly half the sales despite representing just 25% of total transactions, proving that capturing more sales in higher-priced items is the clearest path to sustained growth and profitability.

So long as households continue to look for ways to make their budgets go further, Dollar Tree appears well-positioned to benefit as it becomes a more relevant everyday shopping destination for consumers across income levels.

#2899. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.
